questions.stem: The side chains of four amino acids are considered: serine bears a hydroxyl group, alanine bears a methyl group, aspartic acid bears a second carboxyl group, and lysine bears a terminal amino group. Which statement is correct?
options: Serine and alanine belong together to the polar, uncharged class.
At pH 7, aspartic acid carries a net negative charge and lysine carries a net positive charge.
Aspartic acid is basic, because its extra carboxyl group accepts protons at pH 7.
Lysine is acidic, because its terminal amino group releases protons readily at pH 7.
All four side chains are uncharged at pH 7.
questions.exp: A carboxyl side chain loses its proton well below pH 7, so aspartate is negative there, while the amino group of lysine stays protonated and positive. The option that calls carboxyl groups proton acceptors reverses their acid behaviour, and alanine's methyl side chain makes it nonpolar rather than polar.

questions.stem: A tripeptide is assembled in the order glutamic acid, glycine, lysine. Peptide bonds are not ionisable, and the only groups carrying charge near pH 7 are the terminal amino and carboxyl groups plus the side chains of the glutamic and lysine residues. What is the net charge of this tripeptide at pH 7?
questions.exp: At pH 7 the N-terminal amino group and the lysine side chain are protonated, giving +2 in total, while the C-terminal carboxyl group and the glutamate side chain are deprotonated, giving -2, so the net charge is zero. The +2 option counts only the positive groups and forgets the two deprotonated ones.
questions.topic: Biology · ionisation of peptides at pH

questions.stem: Collagen aside, proline is rarely found in the middle of an alpha helix. The best explanation is that proline:
options: carries a charged side chain that repels the peptide backbone
cannot form peptide bonds with the residues on either side
is nonpolar, and alpha helices form only around polar side chains
has its side chain bonded back to the backbone nitrogen, so it cannot donate the helix hydrogen bond
is too small to reach across one full turn of the helix
questions.exp: Proline is a secondary amine: its side chain ties up the backbone nitrogen, so the N-H that should donate the helix hydrogen bond is missing and the rigid ring introduces a kink. The nonpolar option fails because many nonpolar residues such as alanine and leucine sit comfortably inside helices; the problem is the missing N-H, not the polarity.

questions.stem: A reagent breaks the four intrachain disulfide bridges of a protein made of a single polypeptide chain, without touching any peptide bond. Which levels of protein structure are directly lost, and which are preserved?
options: Tertiary structure is directly lost; the primary structure is fully preserved.
Primary and tertiary structures are lost; the secondary structure is preserved.
Secondary structure is directly lost; the tertiary structure is preserved.
All four levels of structure are lost, including the primary sequence.
Quaternary structure is lost, because disulfide bridges are the bonds that hold separate chains together.
questions.exp: Disulfide bridges lock the folded tertiary shape in place, so cutting them unfolds the chain while the covalent amino acid sequence survives. A single chain has no quaternary level to lose, and the option that loses the primary structure mistakes disulfide bridges for peptide bonds.
questions.topic: Biology · disulfide bonds and tertiary structure

questions.stem: Two synthetic peptides of equal length adopt different secondary structures: peptide P forms an alpha helix and peptide Q forms an antiparallel beta sheet. Which statement is correct?
options: Both structures are stabilised by covalent bonds between side chains.
In peptide P the hydrogen bonds form between side chains, while in peptide Q they form along the backbone.
In peptide P the backbone hydrogen bonds run between neighbouring strands, while in peptide Q they run within one chain.
Neither structure uses hydrogen bonds: peptide P is held by disulfide bridges and peptide Q by ionic bonds.
In peptide P the hydrogen bonds join backbone atoms within the same chain, while in peptide Q they join backbone atoms of neighbouring strands.
questions.exp: Both structures are built from hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups: within one chain, four residues apart, in an alpha helix, and across adjacent strands in a beta sheet. The side-chain option fails because the regular hydrogen-bonding pattern that holds either structure uses backbone atoms, and all these bonds are noncovalent.
questions.topic: Biology · alpha helix vs beta sheet

questions.stem: A newly characterised protein is a long, water-insoluble strand that gives tendon its tensile strength and forms insoluble fibres outside the body. Which classification and justification are correct?
options: Globular, because tendon proteins need a compact soluble shape to transmit force.
Fibrous, because long insoluble strands with a mechanical role are the hallmark of fibrous proteins such as collagen.
Conjugated, because an insoluble protein must carry a non-protein prosthetic group.
Globular, because every structural protein is globular and only metabolic proteins are fibrous.
Fibrous, because all proteins found outside cells are fibrous.
questions.exp: Shape and role decide the class: fibrous proteins are long, insoluble strands with structural functions (collagen, keratin), while globular proteins are compact and soluble (enzymes, transport proteins). The extracellular-location option fails because albumin works outside cells yet is a soluble globular protein.

questions.stem: Which statement about levels of protein structure is correct?
options: Quaternary structure is present in every protein that contains more than one amino acid.
The primary structure of a protein is the ordered list of its alpha helices and beta sheets.
Tertiary structure is stabilised only by the sequence and never by interactions between side chains.
Replacing a single amino acid in the primary structure can change the tertiary structure of the whole chain.
Hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms define the tertiary structure rather than the secondary structure.
questions.exp: The side-chain interactions that build the tertiary fold are dictated by the sequence, so one substitution, classically in sickle-cell haemoglobin, can remodel the fold or the behaviour of the whole protein. Quaternary structure requires several separate polypeptide chains, not merely many residues, and backbone hydrogen bonds are the hallmark of secondary structure.

questions.stem: Cellulose and starch are both polymers of glucose, yet cellulose passes through the human gut largely undigested. The reason is that:
options: cellulose is built from fructose units that the human gut cannot absorb
cellulose is unbranched, and no enzyme anywhere can attack an unbranched glucose chain
cellulose is joined by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds, and humans lack cellulase, the enzyme that hydrolyses them
cellulose repels water so strongly that digestive enzymes cannot reach its bonds
cellulose molecules are too long to be broken down by any organism
questions.exp: The two polymers differ in the geometry of the glycosidic bond: human amylase handles the alpha linkages of starch, but the beta-1,4 bonds of cellulose require cellulase, which humans do not secrete. Ruminants digest cellulose only with help from symbiotic microbes, so the too-long-for-any-organism option fails.

questions.stem: Muscle glycogen releases usable glucose units faster than the amylopectin of a starchy meal, although both are branched polymers of alpha-glucose. The best explanation is that glycogen:
options: is more highly branched than amylopectin, so many more non-reducing ends can be attacked at the same time by the mobilising enzymes
contains some beta bonds that are hydrolysed faster than alpha bonds
is first converted to fat, which diffuses through the muscle faster than glucose
is a smaller molecule, so fewer glycosidic bonds need to be broken per gram
is partly digested by salivary amylase before it reaches the muscle
questions.exp: Branching multiplies the number of chain ends: glycogen phosphorylase and the debranching system work from the non-reducing ends, and a densely branched polymer offers far more ends in parallel than amylopectin. The beta-bond option fails because both polymers are alpha-glucose polymers, and muscle mobilises its own glycogen inside the cell with no digestive enzyme involved.

questions.stem: In a chromatogram of a leaf extract, the yellow-orange bands contain carotenes and xanthophylls. Which statement about these pigments is correct?
options: They are water-soluble proteins that transfer electrons to photosystem II.
They are breakdown products of chlorophyll a that have lost their magnesium atom.
They are water-soluble pigments dissolved in the stroma of the chloroplast.
They are lipid-soluble accessory pigments of the thylakoid membranes, and xanthophylls are oxygen-containing carotenoids.
They are lipid-soluble pigments that absorb light only in the infrared range.
questions.exp: Carotenes are hydrocarbons and xanthophylls their oxygenated derivatives; both are lipid-soluble carotenoids embedded in the thylakoid membranes, where they broaden light capture and help dissipate excess energy. They are distinct molecules from chlorophyll, not its degradation products, and they absorb in the visible range, not the infrared.

questions.stem: Per gram, fat stores about twice as much usable energy as glycogen. Which statement explains this most directly?
options: Fat cells store more water than glycogen deposits, and the water raises the energy yield.
Fats contain more peptide bonds per gram than carbohydrates.
The long hydrocarbon chains of fatty acids are highly reduced, and triglycerides are stored almost without water, while glycogen binds a large mass of water.
Glycogen is chemically a lipid, and its branching makes it less efficient.
Fat is oxidised anaerobically, so none of its energy is lost as heat.
questions.exp: Energy yield per gram tracks the reduction state of the molecule: the many C-H bonds of fatty acid chains oxidise to release more energy than the partially oxidised glucose units, and triglyceride droplets carry no stored water, whereas hydrated glycogen pays a large water mass penalty. Fat oxidation is aerobic, so the anaerobic option fails.

questions.stem: Starch is incubated with purified amylase under gut-like conditions, and the mixture then meets the brush-border enzymes of the small intestine. Which statement describes the carbohydrate products of the two stages correctly?
options: Amylase releases free glucose from starch, and the brush-border enzymes then split glucose into smaller sugars.
Amylase digests starch only to water and carbon dioxide; the brush-border enzymes finish the job.
Starch digestion cannot begin until bacteria in the large intestine supply the needed amylase.
Amylase mainly releases maltose and similar short chains, and the brush-border disaccharidases then release the monosaccharides.
Amylase converts starch into lactose, and brush-border lactase then splits the lactose.
questions.exp: Amylase hydrolyses the alpha-1,4 bonds of starch but stops at short products, so its output is maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins rather than free glucose; membrane-bound maltase, isomaltase and sucrase then release the monosaccharides. The direct-glucose option is the classic error, and lactose is a milk sugar that starch cannot yield.

questions.stem: Lactose, the disaccharide in milk, is hydrolysed at the intestinal brush border by lactase. The correct reaction is:
options: lactose + water → glucose + galactose
lactose + water → glucose + fructose
lactose + water → glucose + glucose
lactose → glucose + galactose, with water released
lactose + water → galactose + galactose
questions.exp: Lactose is glucose joined to galactose, so hydrolysis consumes water and releases both monosaccharides. The glucose-plus-fructose option describes sucrose digestion, the two-glucose option describes maltose, and hydrolysis uses water rather than releasing it.

questions.stem: In a tube containing enzyme and a large excess of its substrate, the enzyme concentration is doubled while temperature and pH are held constant. The initial reaction rate will:
options: fall to half, because the substrate is now shared among more active sites
stay the same, because enzymes are not consumed by the reaction
double, because with substrate in excess the initial rate is proportional to the enzyme concentration
double immediately and then double again every few minutes
drop to zero, because excess substrate competes with the enzyme
questions.exp: At saturating substrate every enzyme molecule already works at its maximum turnover, so doubling the number of enzyme molecules doubles the total rate. The not-consumed option confuses the enzyme's persistence with the capacity of the enzyme amount present.

questions.stem: Two tubes contain the same small, fixed amount of substrate. Tube X receives 1 unit of enzyme and tube Y receives 4 units of the same enzyme; temperature and pH are equal and optimal. Which outcome is expected?
options: Tube Y yields four times the final amount of product that tube X yields.
Tube X yields more product in the end, because its substrate lasts longer.
Neither tube produces product, because the substrate amount is below the saturation point.
Tube Y reacts more slowly at first and then overtakes tube X near the end.
Both tubes yield the same final amount of product, but tube Y reaches it sooner.
questions.exp: Enzyme concentration sets the speed, not the ceiling: with the substrate amount fixed, both tubes approach the same total product, and the tube with four times the enzyme arrives sooner. The four-times-product option wrongly multiplies the yield by the rate factor.
questions.topic: Biology · enzyme amount vs substrate amount

questions.stem: An enzyme is added to a reaction mixture that has already reached chemical equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
options: The enzyme pushes the equilibrium toward the products and raises the final yield.
The enzyme lowers the activation energy of both directions, so equilibrium is reached sooner at the same position.
The enzyme lowers the activation energy of the forward direction only.
The enzyme increases the energy difference between reactants and products.
The enzyme is gradually consumed, so the mixture returns to its original state.
questions.exp: Catalysts reduce the activation barrier equally for the forward and reverse steps, so both rates rise while the equilibrium composition, which depends only on the relative energies of the states, is untouched. The yield-raising option confuses a faster approach to equilibrium with a different end point.

questions.stem: In prion diseases, a misfolded form of a normal membrane protein acts as a template: contact converts the normal form into the misfolded shape, which then joins growing aggregates. Which statement follows from this mechanism?
options: Each converted molecule becomes a new template that converts others, so the number of misfolded molecules can grow exponentially without any nucleic acid.
The misfolded protein carries a nucleic acid sequence that mutates the DNA of the cells it enters.
The aggregates are composed of lipid that has been misread from membrane phospholipids.
The process requires a virus to replicate, because no protein can propagate information alone.
The reaction is self-limiting, because one misfolded molecule can convert at most one other molecule in its lifetime.
questions.exp: Templated misfolding is autocatalytic: every newly converted molecule is itself infectious material, so the misfolded population can grow exponentially even though prions contain no nucleic acid. The one-to-one option ignores the chain reaction, and the virus option fails because protein conformation alone transmits the information.

questions.stem: A cell line carries a mutation that disables its main chaperone proteins, while protein synthesis continues normally and amino acid sequences are unchanged. The most likely consequence inside the cell is that:
options: the primary structure of each new protein is edited, because chaperones remove wrong amino acids during folding
new proteins are exported while still unfolded, because folding normally happens outside the cell
ribosomes stop translating, because chaperones supply the energy for peptide bond formation
many new chains expose their hydrophobic regions, bind each other, and aggregate instead of reaching the native fold
nothing changes, because the amino acid sequence alone always guarantees correct folding inside a living cell
questions.exp: Chaperones shield exposed hydrophobic patches and give new chains time to find the native fold, so without them those patches stick to one another and aggregates form. The sequence itself is untouched because chaperones affect conformation, not covalent structure, and the do-nothing option ignores that aggregation competes with folding in the crowded cell.

questions.stem: In a steroid-producing gland cell, the smooth endoplasmic reticulum is actively making hormones, while a lysosome is digesting a bacterium taken in by phagocytosis. Which pair of products is formed by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and by lysosomal action, respectively?
options: Peptide hormones by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum; small soluble digestion products such as amino acids and monosaccharides by the lysosome.
Steroid hormones by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum; small soluble digestion products such as amino acids and monosaccharides by the lysosome.
Steroid hormones by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum; hydrogen peroxide and water by the lysosome.
Steroid hormones by the rough endoplasmic reticulum; intact bacterial fragments kept permanently inside the lysosome.
Steroid hormones by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum; fully digested proteins exported out of the cell by the lysosome.
questions.exp: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is the site of lipid and steroid synthesis, so the gland's product is a steroid, while lysosomal acid hydrolases break the bacterium down into small soluble molecules that pass into the cytosol. The peptide-hormone option belongs to rough-ER products, and the hydrogen-peroxide option describes peroxisomes, not lysosomes.
questions.topic: Biology · products of smooth ER and lysosome action

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about peroxisomes and lysosomes is correct?
options: Peroxisomal catalase decomposes the hydrogen peroxide formed inside the organelle into water and oxygen.
Lysosomes generate hydrogen peroxide while oxidising fatty acids and amino acids.
Peroxisomes are formed as vesicles budding from the Golgi apparatus and are filled with acid hydrolases.
The interior of peroxisomes is strongly acidic, which is the optimum for catalase.
Lysosomal hydrolases convert hydrogen peroxide into water and molecular oxygen.
questions.exp: Oxidases inside peroxisomes produce hydrogen peroxide, and catalase, also located in the peroxisome, splits it into water and oxygen. The hydrogen-peroxide options misplace this reaction in lysosomes, the Golgi-derived vesicles filled with acid hydrolases are lysosomes, and the strongly acidic interior belongs to the lysosome rather than the peroxisome.

questions.stem: In animal cells the first step of peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation is catalysed by an oxidase that passes electrons directly to oxygen, forming hydrogen peroxide. A mutation abolishes the activity of peroxisomal catalase. Which outcome is expected?
options: Fatty acid oxidation in the peroxisome stops immediately, because catalase performs the first oxidation step.
Hydrogen peroxide is delivered to lysosomes, where hydrolases split it safely into water and oxygen.
Hydrogen peroxide leaves the cell unchanged at a rate that fully protects the cytosol.
Hydrogen peroxide generated in the peroxisome is no longer decomposed, so it accumulates and can reach the cytosol, where it damages cellular components.
The mitochondrion takes over the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide at the cost of extra ATP consumption.
questions.exp: Catalase normally splits the peroxide produced by peroxisomal oxidases into water and oxygen; without it the peroxide accumulates and, being a small uncharged molecule, can diffuse out and oxidise cytosolic components. The first-step option is wrong because the oxidase, not catalase, performs that step, and lysosomes carry hydrolases, not peroxide-splitting catalase.

questions.stem: A metabolic poison halts ATP production in an animal cell kept in an isotonic medium. Which combination of transport processes continues at its normal rate for some time?
options: Sodium-potassium pumping out of the cell continues, while osmosis through aquaporins stops.
Facilitated diffusion of glucose down its concentration gradient and osmosis of water continue, while sodium-potassium pumping stops.
Every carrier-mediated process stops, because all carrier proteins are driven directly by ATP hydrolysis.
Active uptake of calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum continues, while osmosis stops.
Sodium-potassium pumping and osmosis continue, while facilitated diffusion of glucose stops.
questions.exp: Osmosis and facilitated diffusion are passive and run without ATP, whereas the sodium-potassium pump and the calcium pump of the endoplasmic reticulum hydrolyse ATP directly and stop first. The claim that all carrier-mediated transport needs ATP confuses active transport with passive carrier-mediated diffusion.

questions.stem: Cells are cultured in a medium whose glucose concentration is higher than the glucose concentration inside the cells. The cells take up glucose through a membrane carrier protein, and the uptake rate is unchanged when ATP synthesis is blocked by a poison. Which process accounts for the uptake?
options: Simple diffusion through the phospholipid bilayer
Primary active transport coupled to ATP hydrolysis
Facilitated diffusion through the carrier protein
Secondary active transport driven by the sodium gradient
Endocytosis of glucose in membrane vesicles
questions.exp: Glucose moves down its concentration gradient through a specific carrier and proceeds without ATP, which is exactly facilitated diffusion; glucose is polar and cannot cross the bilayer by simple diffusion. The active-transport options would slow or stop when ATP production is blocked, and glucose uptake here needs no sodium gradient.

questions.stem: A red blood cell whose interior behaves as 300 mmol/dm³ of non-penetrating solute is placed in a large volume of solution containing 150 mmol/dm³ sodium chloride (fully dissociated) and 100 mmol/dm³ urea. Sodium chloride cannot cross the membrane; urea crosses freely. What happens to the cell?
options: Water first leaves the cell and it shrinks; once urea has equilibrated across the membrane, water returns and the cell regains its original volume.
Water first leaves the cell and it shrinks; later, water re-enters and the cell swells until it lyses.
No net movement of water occurs at any time, because the sodium chloride by itself is already isotonic with the cytosol.
Water enters the cell continuously from the start and the cell lyses, because the outside solution has the higher total concentration of solute particles.
The cell shrinks permanently, because urea that has entered the cytosol cannot leave again.
questions.exp: The solution initially exerts about 400 mmol/dm³ of particles against 300 inside, so water leaves and the cell shrinks. Urea then diffuses in down its gradient until both sides hold 100 mmol/dm³, water follows back, and the cell returns to its original volume, since 300 fixed particles plus 100 urea inside now match 300 plus 100 outside. The lysis outcome would apply to a penetrating solute without any non-penetrating salt, and the no-movement option ignores the initial excess of urea.
questions.topic: Biology · osmosis with a penetrating solute

questions.stem: Which statement about the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane is correct?
options: The membrane is a rigid structure in which every protein is fixed in one position for the life of the cell.
The hydrophobic fatty acid tails of the phospholipids face the aqueous solutions on both sides of the membrane.
The core of the bilayer is hydrophilic, which is why small ions cross it freely.
Cholesterol is the main component of plant-cell membranes and is absent from animal cells.
Phospholipids and many membrane proteins can move laterally within the bilayer, which behaves as a two-dimensional fluid.
questions.exp: In the fluid mosaic model the bilayer is a two-dimensional fluid in which lipids and many proteins diffuse laterally, with proteins embedded as a mosaic. The tails face inward, the hydrophobic core actually blocks ions, and cholesterol is a characteristic component of animal-cell membranes rather than being absent from them.

questions.stem: Researchers treat sealed vesicles of plasma membrane in two ways. Treatment 1 uses a concentrated salt solution that disrupts ionic and polar interactions but leaves the bilayer intact. Treatment 2 uses a mild detergent that dissolves the bilayer. Which result is expected?
options: Treatment 1 releases peripheral proteins bound to the membrane surfaces, while treatment 2 releases integral proteins such as transmembrane channels.
Treatment 1 releases integral proteins, because their transmembrane segments bind ions, while treatment 2 releases only peripheral proteins.
Both treatments release only peripheral proteins, because integral proteins are protected by carbohydrate chains.
Neither treatment can release integral proteins, because transmembrane segments cannot be separated from lipids.
Treatment 1 releases both classes of protein equally, because ionic interactions anchor the integral proteins in the bilayer.
questions.exp: Peripheral proteins attach to the membrane surface through ionic and polar interactions and come away with high salt, while integral proteins are anchored by hydrophobic transmembrane segments and are freed only when detergent disrupts the bilayer. The option claiming ionic anchoring reverses the chemistry: the transmembrane anchor is hydrophobic, not ionic.

questions.stem: A red blood cell is moved from an isotonic medium into a solution with a higher total concentration of non-penetrating solutes than the cytosol. What is the outcome?
options: Water enters the cell by osmosis and the cell swells.
Water leaves the cell by osmosis and the cell shrivels.
Non-penetrating solutes enter the cell until the two concentrations are equal, so the volume stays constant.
The volume stays constant, because a cell wall resists any change in water content.
Water leaves the cell until the membrane bursts.
questions.exp: The hypertonic medium draws water out by osmosis, so the animal cell shrivels. The bursting outcome belongs to the opposite case, a hypotonic medium, red blood cells have no cell wall, and non-penetrating solutes cannot cross the membrane to equalise the concentrations.

questions.stem: Cells from the same tissue are divided into two samples: one sample is placed in solution X, which is hypertonic to the cells, and the other in solution Y, which is hypotonic to the cells. Both plant and animal cells are treated this way. Which statement about the outcomes is correct?
options: In solution X the plant cells show plasmolysis, with the plasma membrane pulling away from the intact wall, while in solution Y the animal cells swell and may burst.
In solution X both cell types burst, while in solution Y both cell types shrink.
In solution X the plant cell walls collapse inward together with the membrane, while in solution Y the animal cells become turgid.
In solution X the animal cells become turgid, while in solution Y the plant cells show plasmolysis.
In solution X the animal cells remain unchanged because their membrane is elastic, while in solution Y the plant cells burst.
questions.exp: In the hypertonic solution water leaves: the plant protoplast shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the rigid wall, which itself does not collapse, while the animal cell simply shrivels. In the hypotonic solution water flows in: the wall lets the plant cell build turgor pressure without bursting, whereas the wall-less animal cell swells and may lyse.
questions.topic: Biology · tonicity in plant vs animal cells

questions.stem: Viruses are described as acellular. Which statement gives the main reason?
options: A virus particle contains either DNA or RNA, but never both at once.
A virus has no cytoplasm, no ribosomes and no metabolism of its own, and it can multiply only inside a host cell.
A virus particle is far too small to be seen with a light microscope.
A virus has no cell wall around its nucleic acid.
A virus can be crystallised and stored like a chemical substance.
questions.exp: A virus lacks cytoplasm, ribosomes and independent metabolism, and it reproduces only by hijacking a host cell, so it satisfies none of the defining features of a cell. The single-genome statement is a true property of viruses but not the reason they are acellular, and small size or crystallisation do not define cellularity.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about viruses is correct?
options: The envelope of an enveloped virus is assembled on its own ribosomes from lipids synthesised by viral enzymes.
A single virus particle may contain one DNA genome and one RNA genome at the same time.
Viruses increase in number by binary fission within the host cytoplasm.
An enveloped virus takes its lipid envelope from a host-cell membrane as it leaves the cell and inserts its own glycoproteins into that envelope.
Viruses carry ribosomes that switch on only after the nucleic acid has entered the host cell.
questions.exp: Enveloped viruses obtain their lipid envelope from host membranes during budding or exocytosis and embed virus-encoded glycoproteins in it. Viruses never hold two genome types at once, possess no ribosomes at all, and binary fission is a cellular process they do not perform.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a plastid type with what it stores is correct?
options: Amyloplasts store starch, for example in potato tubers.
Elaioplasts store proteins, for example in cereal grains.
Aleuroplasts store oils and lipids, for example in oil seeds.
Chromoplasts store chlorophyll, for example in mature leaves.
Amyloplasts store the red and yellow pigments, for example in tomato fruits.
questions.exp: Amyloplasts are starch-storing leucoplasts, elaioplasts store oils and lipids, and aleuroplasts store protein, while the carotenoid pigments of fruit and petals sit in chromoplasts and leaf chlorophyll sits in chloroplasts. The elaioplast and aleuroplast pairings in the other options are swapped.

questions.stem: During the ripening of a tomato fruit the green colour fades, red pigments accumulate, and the starch stored in the fruit is converted into sugars. Which combination of plastid events fits these changes?
options: Chloroplasts differentiate into amyloplasts as starch accumulates, while chromoplasts break the sugars down further.
Elaioplasts differentiate into chloroplasts as chlorophyll returns, while aleuroplasts release carotenoids.
Chloroplasts differentiate into chromoplasts as carotenoids accumulate, while amyloplasts release the starch that is hydrolysed to sugars.
Chromoplasts differentiate back into chloroplasts as the fruit ripens, while elaioplasts hydrolyse the starch.
Chloroplasts differentiate into leucoplasts that store the red pigments, while amyloplasts build new starch from the sugars.
questions.exp: In ripening fruit, chloroplasts change into chromoplasts, which accumulate the red carotenoid lycopene, and the starch held in amyloplasts is hydrolysed to sugars that sweeten the tissue. The reversed-conversion options get the direction of differentiation wrong, and carotenoids are stored in chromoplasts rather than in leucoplasts or elaioplasts.

questions.stem: In Tay-Sachs disease, a defective gene leaves one enzyme inactive inside a particular organelle. Nerve cells of affected children develop swollen vesicles packed with undigested ganglioside lipids. Which statement identifies the organelle and explains the accumulation?
options: The peroxisome lacks catalase, so lipids taken in for oxidation accumulate inside it.
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum overproduces lipids faster than they can be exported, so lipid-filled vesicles swell up.
The lysosome lacks a functional hydrolytic enzyme, so lipid delivered to it for digestion is not broken down and accumulates inside it.
The Golgi apparatus fails to package secretory proteins, so undigested lipid collects in secretory vesicles.
The mitochondrion cannot oxidise the gangliosides, so the lipid is stored inside mitochondrial cristae.
questions.exp: Tay-Sachs is a lysosomal storage disease: a defective acid hydrolase cannot degrade gangliosides, so the lipid delivered to lysosomes for digestion accumulates in swollen vesicles. The peroxisome performs oxidation reactions such as very-long-chain fatty acid breakdown, not ganglioside digestion, and the ER and Golgi options describe synthesis and packaging steps that are not the defect.

questions.stem: Three treatments each disable one organelle in a cell line. After treatment 1, secreted proteins are synthesised but are never given mature carbohydrate chains and are not sorted to their destinations. After treatment 2, the cells cannot break down very-long-chain fatty acids. After treatment 3, engulfed bacteria are not digested even though acid hydrolases are produced normally. Which set of organelles is disabled by treatments 1, 2 and 3, respectively?
options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum; lysosome; peroxisome
Golgi apparatus; lysosome; peroxisome
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum; peroxisome; Golgi apparatus
Rough endoplasmic reticulum; peroxisome; lysosome
Golgi apparatus; peroxisome; lysosome
questions.exp: The Golgi apparatus matures carbohydrate chains and sorts proteins for export, the peroxisome houses the breakdown of very-long-chain fatty acids, and lysosomes provide the acid hydrolases that digest engulfed bacteria. Sorting to final destinations is a Golgi function, so the rough-ER option for treatment 1 is not the best match even though the first glycosylation step happens there, and the option assigning the lysosome to the fatty-acid defect swaps peroxisomal oxidation for lysosomal digestion.

questions.stem: A bacterial culture is treated with a drug that completely inhibits DNA gyrase, a topoisomerase. Helicase and DNA polymerase are unaffected, and replication was already under way at several forks when the drug was added. Which outcome is expected?
options: Replication continues at normal speed, because topoisomerase acts only at the very end of replication to link the two daughter molecules.
Replication forks stall shortly after drug addition, because unwinding by helicase leaves the unreplicated DNA ahead of each fork increasingly overwound and torsionally strained.
Helicase can no longer separate the two strands, because topoisomerase is the enzyme that breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.
Okazaki fragments accumulate on the lagging strand, because topoisomerase normally seals the nicks between adjacent fragments.
The separated parental strands cannot act as templates, because topoisomerase proofreads newly synthesized DNA.
questions.exp: Topoisomerase relieves the positive supercoiling that builds up ahead of a moving fork; without it the torsional strain rapidly blocks helicase, so forks stall even though helicase and polymerase themselves are intact. The Okazaki option describes the job of DNA ligase, which seals nicks between fragments and is a different enzyme.

questions.stem: In a temperature-sensitive bacterial mutant shifted to the restrictive temperature, DNA ligase is inactive while helicase, primase and DNA polymerase still function normally. Which observation is expected in cells that were replicating at the time of the shift?
options: The lagging strand remains as a series of separate Okazaki fragments, because the nicks between adjacent fragments are not sealed.
The leading strand also remains in fragments, because ligase normally cuts the leading strand into pieces during replication.
Helicase stops unwinding the parental double helix, because the torsional stress generated by unwinding can only be resolved by ligase.
No new Okazaki fragments are synthesized at all, because the synthesis of each fragment requires ligase.
RNA primers are no longer removed from the fragments, because primer removal is carried out by DNA ligase.
questions.exp: Primase and polymerase make each Okazaki fragment, so fragments still form at the restrictive temperature; ligase only forms the final phosphodiester bond between adjacent fragments, so the lagging strand stays discontinuous. The helicase option assigns ligase the torsion-relieving role that belongs to topoisomerase.

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic species, nucleosomes are arranged with a repeat length of 200 bp of DNA per nucleosome. Each nucleosome core particle contains two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, with 147 bp of DNA wrapped around the octamer. A linear stretch of this chromatin is 24,000 bp long. How many molecules of histone H3 are present in its nucleosome core particles?
options: 60 molecules
120 molecules
240 molecules
480 molecules
960 molecules
questions.exp: The stretch holds 24000 / 200 = 120 core particles, and each core particle contains two H3 molecules, giving 2 x 120 = 240. The 480 option counts all four core histone types as if each contributed H3, and the 960 option counts every protein in the octamer as H3.

questions.stem: Which statement about histones is correct?
options: Histones are acidic proteins that bind DNA through attraction between their negatively charged side chains and the positively charged DNA backbone.
Histones are covalently joined to DNA by a ligation reaction, which is what holds each nucleosome together.
Bacterial chromosomes are organized around histone octamers in the same way as eukaryotic chromosomes.
Histones are small basic proteins whose positive charges bind the negatively charged phosphate groups of the DNA backbone.
Each nucleosome core particle contains eight different histone types, one molecule of each kind.
questions.exp: Histones are rich in lysine and arginine, so they are basic and bind the acidic phosphate backbone mainly through ionic interactions, not covalent bonds. The acidic-protein option reverses the charge logic: acidic side chains would repel the DNA phosphates rather than attract them.

questions.stem: Bacteria are grown for many generations in a medium whose only nitrogen source is the heavy isotope 15N, so that all their DNA is fully heavy. The culture is then transferred to ordinary 14N medium and allowed to complete three further rounds of replication. Assuming semiconservative replication, what fraction of the double-stranded DNA molecules present at the end contain 15N in at least one of their strands?
questions.exp: The two original heavy strands never disappear: in every generation each sits in exactly one hybrid molecule, so there are always 2 molecules containing 15N, while the total number of molecules doubles each round. After three rounds there are 8 molecules, so the fraction is 2/8 = 1/4; the answer 3/4 is the fraction that is entirely new instead.

questions.stem: In a Meselson-Stahl type experiment, bacteria grown in 15N medium are shifted to 14N medium and allowed to replicate for exactly two rounds. Centrifugation then separates the DNA into two distinct bands: one at intermediate density and one fully light, with no heavy band anywhere in the tube. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Semiconservative replication is excluded, because it predicts a single intermediate band after two rounds.
Only the conservative model is excluded, because the dispersive model still predicts two separate bands.
Only the dispersive model is excluded, because the conservative model still predicts an intermediate band.
Both the conservative and the dispersive models are excluded, which is the classic evidence for semiconservative replication.
The experiment is uninterpretable, because no model predicts a light band after only two rounds.
questions.exp: After two rounds semiconservative replication gives half hybrid molecules (the intermediate band) and half fully light molecules (the light band). The conservative model would still show a fully heavy band, and the dispersive model would give one single band of uniform intermediate density, so two bands with no heavy band rule out both rivals at once.

questions.stem: Which statement about the eukaryotic (80S) ribosome is correct?
options: Its large and small subunits are assembled in the nucleolus and are exported separately to the cytoplasm, where they combine only when translation begins.
The complete 80S particle is assembled in the cytoplasm on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
It is built from a 50S large subunit and a 30S small subunit, as is the case in all living cells.
One of its subunits is made of protein only and the other of RNA only.
Its subunits are assembled in the Golgi apparatus and delivered to the cytoplasm inside transport vesicles.
questions.exp: Ribosomal RNA is transcribed and the subunits begin assembling in the nucleolus; the mature 60S and 40S subunits are then exported separately and only associate on an mRNA at initiation. The 50S plus 30S option describes the prokaryotic 70S ribosome, not the eukaryotic one.
questions.topic: Biology · eukaryotic ribosome structure and assembly

questions.stem: A eukaryotic gene consists of two exons separated by one intron, and that intron contains a stop codon in the reading frame. The DNA of the gene, intron included, is inserted into a bacterium under the control of a bacterial promoter, transcribed and translated. Which outcome is expected?
options: The normal-length protein is produced, because bacteria remove introns from RNA using the same spliceosome as eukaryotes.
No polypeptide is produced, because a bacterial ribosome cannot translate a transcript that contains intron sequences.
A protein longer than the normal one is produced, because the entire intron is translated in addition to both exons.
The normal protein is produced, with the amino acids encoded by the intron simply inserted between the two exons.
A shortened polypeptide is produced, because translation stops at the stop codon inside the intron, before the second exon is ever reached.
questions.exp: Prokaryotes generally lack spliceosomes, so the transcript keeps the intron; the ribosome translates exon 1 into the intron and terminates at the in-frame stop codon there, giving a truncated polypeptide that lacks the second exon. The inserted-amino-acids option fails because translation halts inside the intron at that stop codon rather than continuing into exon 2.

questions.stem: Which statement about RNA splicing is correct?
options: Splicing removes the exons and joins the introns together to build the mature mRNA that is translated.
Splicing takes place in the cytoplasm, on the ribosome, immediately before translation begins.
In eukaryotes, introns are removed and exons joined before the mature mRNA leaves the nucleus, whereas most bacterial genes contain no introns and their transcripts are not spliced.
Bacterial mRNAs must be spliced before translation, because bacterial genes are normally rich in introns.
Splicing alters the nucleotide sequence of the exons so that they come to encode different amino acids.
questions.exp: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is spliced in the nucleus before export, and bacterial genes are typically intron-free, so no splicing step exists in bacteria. The first option reverses the two elements: splicing removes introns and joins exons, and it does not change exon sequence.

questions.stem: A codon table shows that CAG codes for glutamine and that UAG is a stop codon. In an mRNA molecule, the codon CAG is changed to UAG by a single base substitution. This mutation is best classified as:
options: A nonsense mutation.
A missense mutation.
A silent mutation.
A frameshift mutation.
An insertion mutation.
questions.exp: The change turns a glutamine codon into a stop signal, so translation ends prematurely and a truncated polypeptide results, which is the definition of a nonsense mutation. A missense classification would require the new codon to specify a different amino acid, and a single base substitution cannot shift the reading frame.

questions.stem: The beginning of an mRNA reads AUG CCU GGU UGA, where UGA is the fourth codon and is a stop signal. Given the code AUG = methionine, CCU = proline, GGU = glycine, ACC = threonine, UGG = tryptophan, UUG = leucine, a mutation inserts one extra nucleotide, A, immediately after the first codon. Which statement is correct?
options: Only one amino acid changes, because the ribosome re-establishes the original reading frame after a single inserted nucleotide.
Methionine is still the first amino acid, but proline, glycine and every later position change, and the original UGA stop signal is never read because it is split across the new codon boundaries.
The protein becomes just methionine followed by threonine, because the new codon ACC acts as a stop signal.
The insertion is silent, because adding a single nucleotide leaves each existing codon intact.
Translation now ends at the position of the former UGA codon, but the amino acids before that point are all unchanged.
questions.exp: Inserting one nucleotide shifts every downstream group of three bases: the new codons are ACC, UGG, UUG, so proline and glycine are replaced by threonine and tryptophan, and the old UGA stop is consumed inside new codons and never read as a stop. The claim that the ribosome restores the frame misses the defining feature of a frameshift: the one-base offset persists to the end of the message.

questions.stem: A codon table gives: GAA and GAG both code for glutamate, GUA codes for valine, and UAA is a stop codon. In the same gene in two different individuals, single-base substitutions occur at the same codon: in mutant X the codon GAA becomes GAG, and in mutant Y the codon GAA becomes GUA. Which classification is correct?
options: X is a missense mutation and Y is a silent mutation.
X is a nonsense mutation and Y is a missense mutation.
X is a silent mutation and Y is a nonsense mutation.
X is a silent mutation and Y is a missense mutation.
X is a frameshift mutation and Y is a missense mutation.
questions.exp: In X the codon still specifies glutamate, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged and the mutation is silent; in Y glutamate is replaced by valine, a different amino acid, so it is missense. The nonsense option is wrong because replacing an acidic residue is not a stop signal: a nonsense mutation needs the codon itself to become a stop codon such as UAA.

questions.stem: A researcher sets up a PCR containing the DNA template, Taq polymerase and all four dNTPs, but accidentally omits the primers. The thermal cycler still runs its full programme of denaturation, annealing and extension. Which outcome is expected?
options: Amplification occurs but more slowly, because Taq polymerase is able to start synthesis on a single-stranded template without a primer.
The dNTPs anneal to the template in place of the missing primers and allow amplification to proceed.
The reaction fails because Taq polymerase is destroyed at the annealing temperature of the cycle.
One copy of the template is produced in each cycle, so the DNA accumulates linearly instead of exponentially.
No amplification occurs, because DNA polymerase cannot start a new strand and can only extend from the free 3' end that a paired primer provides.
questions.exp: Taq polymerase is thermostable but can only add nucleotides to an existing strand, so without oligonucleotide primers supplying a paired 3' end there is no extension step and no product ever accumulates. The linear-accumulation option wrongly assumes that synthesis can begin on a bare single-stranded template.
questions.topic: Biology · PCR components (primers and Taq polymerase)

questions.stem: A PCR tube starts with exactly one double-stranded DNA molecule. The reaction runs three complete cycles, and in every cycle each single strand present serves as the template for one newly synthesized complementary strand. After the third cycle, how many of the double-stranded molecules consist of two newly synthesized strands, with no original template strand at all?
options: 0 molecules
2 molecules
4 molecules
6 molecules
8 molecules
questions.exp: After cycle 1 there are 2 molecules, both hybrids of one old and one new strand; after cycle 2 there are 4 molecules, of which 2 are entirely new; after cycle 3 there are 8 molecules, and only the two strands of the original template still sit in hybrid molecules, leaving 8 - 2 = 6 that are entirely new. The 8 option forgets that each original strand persists in one hybrid molecule forever.

questions.stem: A culture of actively dividing fibroblasts is exposed to UV radiation while all cells are in G1, producing numerous thymine dimers. The G1 checkpoint responds normally. Which outcome is expected?
options: Cells proceed into S phase on schedule, because the G1 checkpoint monitors spindle attachment rather than DNA integrity.
Cells arrest in mitosis, because DNA damage is detected only at the metaphase checkpoint.
Cells arrest in G1 and do not enter S phase until the damage is repaired, so damaged DNA is not replicated.
Cells complete division and enter G0, because DNA repair can occur only after cytokinesis is finished.
Cells replicate the damaged DNA normally in S phase and repair it at the G2 checkpoint before mitosis begins.
questions.exp: The G1 checkpoint halts the cycle while repair systems remove the dimers, so replication of damaged templates is avoided. The claim that the G1 checkpoint monitors spindle attachment confuses it with the metaphase checkpoint, and waiting for repair at G2 would let the dimers be copied first.
questions.topic: Biology · cell cycle checkpoints (G1 DNA damage)

questions.stem: Which statement about the phases of the eukaryotic cell cycle is correct?
options: A cell in the G0 phase actively replicates its DNA in preparation for a future division.
DNA replication takes place during the S phase, so a cell entering mitosis contains twice the amount of DNA it had at the start of interphase.
Chromosome condensation and spindle formation take place during the S phase.
Cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm, is completed during the G2 phase.
The amount of DNA per cell doubles during mitosis and is halved during the S phase.
questions.exp: DNA synthesis occurs only in S phase, so the DNA content is doubled before mitosis begins. The G0 option mistakes a quiescent, non-dividing state for a preparatory one, and condensation plus spindle assembly belong to prophase of the M phase.
questions.topic: Biology · cell cycle phases (G1, S, G2, M, G0)

questions.stem: During an early mitotic division of a chromosomally normal human embryo (2n = 46), the two sister chromatids of chromosome 21 fail to separate in anaphase of one cell. Which outcome is expected in the two daughter cells produced by that division?
options: One daughter cell has 47 chromosomes and the other has 45, so the embryo becomes a mosaic of two cell lines.
Both daughter cells have 47 chromosomes, so the whole embryo becomes trisomic for chromosome 21.
Both daughter cells have 46 chromosomes, because mitotic segregation corrects the failed separation.
One daughter cell has 45 chromosomes and the other has 45, because both copies of chromosome 21 are lost.
One daughter cell has 47 chromosomes and the other has 45, but both lines die so the embryo does not survive.
questions.exp: Both sister chromatids travel to one pole and none to the other, so the daughters are 47 and 45; the monosomic line usually dies while the trisomic line keeps dividing, producing mosaicism. Whole-embryo trisomy arises from a nondisjunction during meiosis, and mitosis has no mechanism that corrects a segregation failure.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about meiosis I is false?
options: During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up in synapsis and may exchange segments by crossing over.
During metaphase I, paired homologous chromosomes align at the equator, with each pair oriented independently of the others.
During anaphase I, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell.
At the end of telophase I, each cell contains half the original chromosome number, and its chromosomes are still made of two sister chromatids.
Meiosis I is called the reductional division because it halves the chromosome number, unlike meiosis II.
questions.exp: In anaphase I, whole homologous chromosomes, each still formed by two sister chromatids, move to opposite poles; centromeres split only in anaphase II. The other statements match meiosis I: synapsis and crossing over in prophase I, random bivalent orientation in metaphase I, and halving of the chromosome number by telophase I.

questions.stem: Crossing over, a major source of new allele combinations, occurs:
options: between the two sister chromatids of the same chromosome during prophase I of meiosis.
between homologous chromosomes during metaphase II, when the pairs align at the equator.
between non-sister chromatids during anaphase II, when the chromatids separate.
between homologous chromosomes during the S phase, while the DNA is being copied.
between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
questions.exp: Chiasmata form while homologues are synapsed in prophase I, and the exchange involves non-sister chromatids of the two homologues. An exchange between sister chromatids would be genetically invisible, because they carry identical alleles.

questions.stem: A plant species has a diploid number of 2n = 10. During anaphase II of meiosis, how many chromosomes move toward each pole, and what does each of them consist of?
options: 10 chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids, move to each pole.
10 chromosomes, each made of a single chromatid, move to each pole.
20 chromatids move as separate chromosomes toward each pole.
5 chromosomes, each made of a single chromatid, move to each pole.
5 chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids, move to each pole.
questions.exp: After meiosis I the secondary meiocyte holds n = 5 double-chromatid chromosomes, and anaphase II splits every centromere, so five single-chromatid chromosomes reach each pole. The options with ten chromosomes per pole ignore the reduction that already occurred in meiosis I.

questions.stem: In a primary spermatocyte with 2n = 12, a nondisjunction of one homologous pair occurs during meiosis I, and meiosis II then proceeds normally. How many of the four resulting gametes have an abnormal chromosome number?
questions.exp: Both cells leaving meiosis I are already unbalanced, one with n+1 = 7 and one with n-1 = 5 chromosomes, and each of them produces two abnormal gametes in meiosis II, so all four gametes are abnormal. The count of two abnormal gametes is the signature of a nondisjunction in meiosis II instead.

questions.stem: A primary spermatocyte (2n = 24) completes meiosis I normally. During meiosis II, in one of the two secondary spermatocytes the sister chromatids of one chromosome fail to separate, while the other secondary spermatocyte divides normally. Which set of sperm is produced?
options: Two sperm with 13 chromosomes and two sperm with 11 chromosomes.
Two sperm with 12 chromosomes, one sperm with 13 and one sperm with 11 chromosomes.
Four sperm with 12 chromosomes each.
One sperm with 12 chromosomes, two sperm with 13 and one sperm with 11 chromosomes.
Two sperm with 24 chromosomes and two sperm with 12 chromosomes.
questions.exp: Only one secondary spermatocyte is affected, so it yields one n+1 sperm (13 chromosomes) and one n-1 sperm (11 chromosomes), while the unaffected one yields two normal sperm with 12. The pattern of two 13s and two 11s would follow from a nondisjunction in meiosis I, where both secondary spermatocytes are already unbalanced.

questions.stem: A male with 2n = 20 produces a sperm sample in which a single nondisjunction event occurred in one meiocyte. The four sperm from that meiocyte carry 11, 10, 10 and 9 chromosomes respectively. In which division did the nondisjunction occur, and why?
options: Meiosis II, because one pair of sister chromatids failed to separate and only one of the two secondary spermatocytes was affected.
Meiosis I, because both cells leaving the first division were already aneuploid.
Meiosis I, because a pair of homologous chromosomes failed to separate and all four sperm are abnormal.
Meiosis II, because the failure of sister chromatids to separate makes all four gametes abnormal.
Either division can be concluded, because both errors produce the same counts of normal and abnormal sperm.
questions.exp: Two normal (10) and two aneuploid (11 and 9) sperm is the signature of a meiosis II error, since only one secondary spermatocyte carries the fault. A meiosis I failure leaves both secondary spermatocytes unbalanced and therefore all four sperm abnormal.

questions.stem: Which statement about the origin of genetic variability in sexually reproducing organisms is correct?
options: Independent assortment occurs during meiosis II, when sister chromatids are distributed at random to the gametes.
Crossing over generates variability by exchanging alleles between the two sister chromatids of a chromosome.
Random fertilisation adds variability because homologous chromosomes exchange segments just before the gametes fuse.
Independent assortment arises because each homologous pair takes a random orientation at the metaphase I plate, independently of every other pair.
Independent assortment can occur only in cells that have first completed crossing over, since unexchanged pairs always segregate identically.
questions.exp: At metaphase I each bivalent attaches to the spindle in a random orientation, so maternal and paternal chromosomes are shuffled independently into the gametes. Crossing over involves non-sister chromatids of homologues, not sister chromatids, and it is independent of, not a requirement for, random bivalent orientation.

questions.stem: In an animal species with 2n = 12, how many genetically different chromosome combinations can the gametes acquire through independent assortment alone, ignoring crossing over?
questions.exp: There are n = 6 homologous pairs and each orients independently at metaphase I, giving 2⁶ = 64 combinations. The value 4096 wrongly raises 2 to the diploid number, and 24 is simply the diploid chromosome count itself.

questions.stem: In humans the M and N blood-group alleles are codominant. A couple are both of type MN. Which phenotype ratio is expected among their children?
options: 3 children of type M for every 1 child of type N
1 child of type M for every 2 children of type MN and 1 child of type N
1 child of type M for every 1 child of type MN and 1 child of type N
2 children of type MN for every 1 child of type M and 1 child of type N
9 children of type M for every 3 children of type MN and 4 children of type N
questions.exp: Two MN parents produce MM, MN and NN offspring in the genotypic ratio 1:2:1, and because the heterozygote is codominant all three genotypes are visible as distinct phenotypes. The 3:1 option would require M to be dominant over N, which codominance rules out.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Mendelian crosses is false?
options: A monohybrid cross between two heterozygous parents gives a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes.
A dihybrid cross between two individuals heterozygous for both genes gives a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio when the genes assort independently.
A testcross between a heterozygous dominant individual and a homozygous recessive partner gives a 1:1 phenotypic ratio.
A cross between two heterozygous parents for a codominant trait gives a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio.
A cross between a homozygous dominant individual and a homozygous recessive partner gives a 1:1 phenotypic ratio.
questions.exp: A homozygous dominant parent crossed with a homozygous recessive one yields only heterozygous offspring, all showing the dominant phenotype. The 1:1 ratio belongs to the testcross with a heterozygous parent, which the other statements describe correctly.

questions.stem: Two pea plants heterozygous for seed shape and for seed colour (AaBb × AaBb) are crossed, and the two genes assort independently. How many different genotypes are expected among the offspring?
questions.exp: Each locus separately gives 3 genotypes (AA, Aa and aa), so the offspring show 3 × 3 = 9 different genotypes, distributed over only 4 phenotype classes. The value 16 counts the Punnett squares, not the distinct genotypes.

questions.stem: In a cross AaBb × aaBb, with the two genes assorting independently, what is expected among the offspring?
options: Four different phenotypes, with one eighth of the offspring showing both recessive traits (aabb).
Four different phenotypes, with one sixteenth of the offspring showing both recessive traits.
Three different phenotypes, with one quarter of the offspring showing both recessive traits.
Two different phenotypes, with one eighth of the offspring showing both recessive traits.
Four different phenotypes, with three sixteenths of the offspring showing both recessive traits.
questions.exp: Aa × aa gives half Aa and half aa, and Bb × Bb gives three quarters B_ and one quarter bb, so the phenotypes are A_B_ (3/8), A_bb (1/8), aaB_ (3/8) and aabb (1/8), four classes in total. The one-sixteenth value would fit a self-fertilisation of a double heterozygote, not this cross.

questions.stem: In a population of 500 people at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 20 people show an autosomal recessive condition (genotype aa). How many people are expected to be heterozygous carriers?
questions.exp: The affected individuals give q² = 20/500 = 0.04, so q = 0.2 and p = 0.8; the carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32, which is 0.32 × 500 = 160 people. The value 80 applies pq = 0.16 and forgets the factor of 2.

questions.stem: A population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and 9 percent of its members show a phenotype caused by a recessive allele. What is the frequency of the dominant allele in this population?
questions.exp: The recessive phenotype marks q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7. The value 0.49 is p², the frequency of homozygous dominant individuals, not of the allele itself.

questions.stem: Which statement about evolution and the history of evolutionary thought is correct?
options: A population bottleneck increases genetic diversity, because only the best-adapted individuals survive the crisis.
Pasteur's swan-necked flask experiment showed that microorganisms appear in nutrient broth only when the broth is exposed to airborne microbes, refuting spontaneous generation.
Pasteur's experiment demonstrated that new species arise through the inheritance of characteristics acquired during an organism's life.
After a bottleneck, the surviving population keeps the allele frequencies of the original population, because which individuals survive is random.
The bottleneck effect generates new alleles, because mutation rates rise when a population becomes small.
questions.exp: Pasteur's curved neck admitted air but trapped microbes and dust, and the broth spoiled only once the neck was broken, so life was shown to arise from existing life. In a bottleneck the small random sample of survivors loses alleles, so heterozygosity falls rather than rises and no new alleles are produced.
questions.topic: Biology · bottleneck effect and spontaneous generation

questions.stem: Which option pairs every site with the epithelium that normally lines it?
options: Alveolus: simple cuboidal; trachea: ciliated pseudostratified columnar; oesophagus: stratified squamous; small intestine: simple columnar
Alveolus: simple squamous; trachea: stratified squamous; oesophagus: stratified squamous; small intestine: simple columnar
Alveolus: simple squamous; trachea: ciliated pseudostratified columnar; oesophagus: stratified squamous; small intestine: simple columnar
Alveolus: simple squamous; trachea: ciliated pseudostratified columnar; oesophagus: transitional; small intestine: simple columnar
Alveolus: simple squamous; trachea: ciliated pseudostratified columnar; oesophagus: stratified squamous; small intestine: simple cuboidal
questions.exp: Alveoli are lined by simple squamous epithelium for rapid diffusion, the trachea by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, the oesophagus by stratified squamous epithelium against abrasion, and the small intestine by simple columnar epithelium for absorption. The tempting alveolus-plus-cuboidal chain overlooks that only the surfactant-secreting type II cells are cuboidal, while the exchange surface itself is the flat type I cell.
questions.topic: Biology · epithelial types and their locations

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about epithelial tissue is false?
options: Epithelia are classified by the number of cell layers and by the shape of the cells at the free surface.
In stratified epithelia the tissue is named for the shape of the cells at the apical surface, not the basal layer.
A gland that develops as an invagination of an epithelium and keeps a duct is still classified as epithelial tissue.
Pseudostratified columnar epithelium is built of several true layers, because only some of its cells reach the free surface.
An epithelium is avascular and takes its nourishment by diffusion from capillaries in the underlying connective tissue.
questions.exp: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium is a single layer: every cell rests on the basement membrane, and the staggered nuclei together with some cells not reaching the free surface create only the illusion of layers. The remaining claims are correct: classification uses layer number plus apical cell shape, ducted glands stay epithelial, and avascular epithelia are fed by diffusion from the tissue beneath.

questions.stem: A light micrograph shows a single layer of tall cells, all resting on the same basement membrane. The nuclei lie at several different heights, giving a layered look, and the free surface carries motile projections. This epithelium is:
options: stratified columnar epithelium lining the oesophagus
ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium lining the trachea
transitional epithelium lining the urinary bladder
simple columnar epithelium with a microvillus border lining the small intestine
stratified squamous epithelium lining the vagina
questions.exp: Nuclei at different heights with every cell still touching the basement membrane define pseudostratified columnar epithelium, and motile surface projections mark it as ciliated, the hallmark lining of the trachea. The stratified columnar option misreads the staggered nuclei as several true layers.

questions.stem: Oxygen travels from the air inside an alveolus into the blood by crossing the alveolar wall and then the capillary wall. Which statement about these exchange surfaces is correct?
options: The alveolar wall is stratified squamous epithelium, because the moving air continually abrades it.
Both walls are simple cuboidal epithelium, whose extra cytoplasm pumps the gases across actively.
The capillary wall is ciliated epithelium, and the cilia propel the blood along the vessel.
The alveolar wall is ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium, a direct continuation of the airway lining.
Both walls are simple squamous epithelium, the thinnest arrangement possible, which keeps the diffusion path short.
questions.exp: Both barriers are simple squamous epithelium, the type I alveolar cells and the capillary endothelium, so the diffusion path from air to blood is as short as possible. The cuboidal option fails because gases diffuse passively and need no pumping cytoplasm, while the ciliated pseudostratified lining belongs to the conducting airways, not to the alveoli.

questions.stem: A toxin selectively destroys the brush border of the cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule, leaving the rest of the nephron intact. Which outcome is expected?
options: Glucose appears in the urine, because the loss of microvilli removes much of the reabsorptive surface and transport capacity of the tubule.
Glomerular filtration stops, because the podocytes of the capsule depend on the same brush border.
Urine volume falls to nearly zero, because most of the filtrate is produced in the proximal tubule.
The collecting duct takes over glucose reabsorption, so the composition of the urine stays normal.
Nothing changes, because microvilli are a feature of the small intestine and not of the kidney.
questions.exp: Proximal tubule cells are simple cuboidal cells with a microvillus brush border that carries the cotransporters reabsorbing essentially all filtered glucose; destroying the border removes that surface, so glucose escapes into the urine while glomerular filtration continues unchanged. The podocyte option confuses the filtration barrier with the tubule lining, and the collecting duct cannot take over glucose reabsorption.

questions.stem: Which nephron segment is correctly matched to its lining epithelium and to the reason that epithelium suits it?
options: Thin limb of the loop of Henle: stratified squamous epithelium, a many-layered wall that resists abrasion by the filtrate.
Proximal convoluted tubule: simple squamous epithelium, whose flat cells make active pumping of glucose faster.
Collecting duct: transitional epithelium, so that the duct can stretch as urine volume rises.
Thin limb of the loop of Henle: simple squamous epithelium, a wall so thin that water and solutes cross it passively with little resistance.
Distal convoluted tubule: ciliated columnar epithelium, whose cilia keep the filtrate well mixed.
questions.exp: The thin limb of the loop of Henle is lined by simple squamous epithelium, ideal for the passive movement of water and solutes on which the counter-current system depends. The proximal tubule option fails on both tissue and logic, since it is simple cuboidal with a brush border for bulk active reabsorption, and transitional epithelium lines the renal pelvis, ureters and bladder, never the nephron itself.

questions.stem: A student wrote the following notes on the surface specializations of epithelial cells. Which note is correct?
options: Cilia contain an actin core and bend through dynein-powered sliding to sweep fluid along the epithelial surface.
Microvilli are non-motile finger-like folds supported by bundles of actin filaments, and they enlarge the absorptive surface of the cell.
Goblet cells release a thin, enzyme-rich secretion that chemically breaks down particles trapped on the epithelium.
Tight junctions anchor the intermediate filaments of neighbouring cells to each other, spreading mechanical stress across the sheet.
The stereocilia of the epididymis beat rhythmically to drive sperm towards the vas deferens.
questions.exp: Microvilli are actin-supported, non-motile folds whose main job is enlarging the apical surface for absorption, as in the intestinal brush border. The cilia note is wrong because cilia are built on a microtubule axoneme rather than actin, goblet cells secrete mucus rather than enzymes, the anchoring of intermediate filaments is the job of desmosomes rather than tight junctions, and epididymal stereocilia do not beat.

questions.stem: In a hereditary disorder the dynein arms of cilia are absent, so cilia cannot beat. Which consequence is expected?
options: Nutrient absorption in the small intestine largely fails, because microvilli use the same dynein motor as cilia.
Mucus clearance is unaffected, because the mucus blanket is dragged along by microvilli rather than cilia.
Mucus accumulates in the airways and transport of the egg along the oviduct is impaired.
Sperm swim normally, because a flagellum is built on a different internal framework from a cilium.
Only the airways are affected, because ciliated cells occur nowhere else in the human body.
questions.exp: Motile cilia in the airways and oviducts and the sperm flagellum all share the same microtubule axoneme driven by dynein, so mucus clearance, egg transport and sperm swimming fail together. Microvilli have an actin core and no dynein, which is why the option blaming failed nutrient absorption is wrong.

questions.stem: A patient's mitral (bicuspid) valve no longer closes completely. What happens during ventricular systole?
options: Blood regurgitates from the aorta back into the left ventricle, so aortic pressure rises.
Blood regurgitates from the left ventricle back into the left atrium, so the stroke volume entering the aorta is reduced.
Blood regurgitates from the right ventricle back into the right atrium, so venous return falls.
The valve cannot open, so the left ventricle fills completely during diastole.
Blood flows from the left atrium into the left ventricle more rapidly during systole.
questions.exp: The mitral valve guards the opening between the left atrium and the left ventricle and must stay shut while that ventricle contracts, so incompetence lets part of the ejected volume leak back into the atrium instead of entering the aorta. The aortic backflow option describes a failing aortic (semilunar) valve, which leaks during diastole, not systole.

questions.stem: The aortic semilunar valve of a patient becomes incompetent, so that it fails to close after ventricular systole. Which combination of effects during ventricular diastole follows?
options: Blood flows from the pulmonary artery into the left ventricle and arterial pressure rises.
Blood flows from the left atrium into the aorta and ventricular filling is prevented.
Blood leaks from the aorta back into the left ventricle, so aortic pressure falls steeply during diastole while the ventricle receives an extra volume of blood.
Blood leaks from the aorta back into the left atrium, so atrial pressure rises.
Blood stays in the aorta because the valve cannot reopen during diastole, so arterial pressure is unchanged.
questions.exp: A semilunar valve must hold up the column of blood in the aorta between beats; if it leaks, blood runs back into the relaxing ventricle, aortic diastolic pressure collapses and the ventricle ends up overfilled before the next contraction. The left-atrium option confuses the aortic valve with the mitral valve, which is the valve that actually separates those two chambers.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a heart valve with its position and its type is correct?
options: The tricuspid valve is a semilunar valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery.
The bicuspid (mitral) valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
The pulmonary valve is an atrioventricular valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
The bicuspid (mitral) valve is an atrioventricular valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
The aortic valve is an atrioventricular valve between the left ventricle and the left atrium.
questions.exp: The two atrioventricular valves sit between atrium and ventricle, tricuspid on the right side and bicuspid (mitral) on the left, while the aortic and pulmonary valves form the semilunar pair at the exits of the ventricles. The tricuspid option misplaces the pulmonary valve and assigns it the wrong class of valve.

questions.stem: A drop of blood enters the heart through the superior vena cava. On its way to the aorta it must pass the following structures: pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle. In which order does it meet them?
options: Right ventricle, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, left atrium, left ventricle.
Right ventricle, pulmonary vein, pulmonary artery, left ventricle, left atrium.
Pulmonary artery, right ventricle, pulmonary vein, left ventricle, left atrium.
Right ventricle, pulmonary artery, left atrium, pulmonary vein, left ventricle.
Left atrium, left ventricle, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, right ventricle.
questions.exp: From the vena cava the blood crosses the right atrium into the right ventricle, leaves by the pulmonary artery for the lungs, returns by the pulmonary veins to the left atrium and finally reaches the left ventricle, whose outflow is the aorta. The option that visits the pulmonary vein before the pulmonary artery reverses the actual direction of pulmonary flow.

questions.stem: A red blood cell leaves the right ventricle and is followed until it re-enters the heart. Which option gives the correct route, with the oxygenation status of the blood at each named stage?
options: Pulmonary artery (oxygenated), lung capillaries, pulmonary vein (deoxygenated), right atrium.
Pulmonary artery (oxygenated), lung capillaries, pulmonary vein (oxygenated), left atrium.
Pulmonary artery (deoxygenated), lung capillaries, pulmonary vein (oxygenated), right atrium.
Pulmonary vein (deoxygenated), lung capillaries, pulmonary artery (oxygenated), left atrium.
Pulmonary artery (deoxygenated), lung capillaries, pulmonary vein (oxygenated), left atrium.
questions.exp: The right ventricle pumps blood out through the pulmonary artery, so the blood is still deoxygenated there; it becomes oxygenated in the lung capillaries and returns by the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The option ending at the right atrium gets the vessels right but sends the blood back to the wrong side of the heart.
questions.topic: Biology · pulmonary circuit (oxygen status of vessels)

questions.stem: Which statement about the human double circulation is correct?
options: The right ventricle has the thickest muscular wall because it serves all the organs of the body.
The right side of the heart pumps blood through the short pulmonary circuit, so blood in the pulmonary arteries travels at a lower pressure than blood in the aorta.
Pulmonary veins carry deoxygenated blood because every vein in the body carries deoxygenated blood.
The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, where the pressure must be high to push blood through the alveolar capillaries.
Systemic arteries and pulmonary arteries both carry oxygenated blood because all arteries leave the heart.
questions.exp: The pulmonary circuit runs only from heart to lungs and back, so it is a short, low-resistance circuit served by the thin-walled right ventricle, and its pressure is far lower than aortic pressure. The blanket rule about veins, and its mirror about arteries, both fail exactly at the pulmonary vessels: pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.
questions.topic: Biology · double circulation (pressure and vessel roles)

questions.stem: At the start of a quiet inhalation the diaphragm contracts. Which chain of events follows?
options: The diaphragm flattens, thoracic volume increases, pressure inside the alveoli falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows inward.
The diaphragm domes upward, thoracic volume increases, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, and air flows inward.
