The diaphragm flattens, thoracic volume decreases, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, and air flows inward.
The diaphragm flattens, thoracic volume increases, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, and air flows outward.
The diaphragm relaxes, thoracic volume decreases, alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows inward.
questions.exp: Contraction pulls the dome of the diaphragm downward so the thoracic cavity enlarges; by the inverse volume-pressure relation the alveolar pressure drops below atmospheric, and air flows down this gradient into the lungs. The option with rising alveolar pressure and inward flow breaks that link, and a relaxing diaphragm belongs to exhalation.

questions.stem: A person blows out a candle forcefully. Which combination of events occurs during this forced exhalation?
options: The diaphragm contracts and alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure.
The abdominal muscles and the internal intercostal muscles contract, the relaxed diaphragm is pushed upward, thoracic volume decreases, and alveolar pressure rises well above atmospheric pressure.
The diaphragm relaxes while the ribs are pulled upward and outward, so thoracic volume increases.
Only the diaphragm relaxes, exactly as in quiet breathing at rest, and no other muscles contribute, so alveolar pressure rises only slightly.
The external intercostal muscles lift the ribs while the diaphragm flattens, so thoracic volume increases.
questions.exp: Forced exhalation is active: abdominal muscles push the relaxed diaphragm up and the internal intercostals pull the ribs down, shrinking thoracic volume below its resting level so alveolar pressure rises well above atmospheric and air is driven out. The upward-and-outward rib movement with a flattening diaphragm is the pattern of inhalation.

questions.stem: Which statement about the pleural membranes is correct?
options: The visceral pleura lines the inside of the chest wall, and the parietal pleura covers the lung surface.
The pleural cavity is a large air-filled space that lets the lungs float freely.
The pleural membranes secrete the mucus that moistens the alveoli for gas exchange.
The pleural cavity normally holds a thin film of serous fluid, so the two layers slide smoothly over each other and the lungs follow the movements of the chest wall.
The pleural cavity contains cartilage rings that keep the bronchi open during breathing.
questions.exp: The parietal layer lines the chest wall and the visceral layer covers the lungs, and between them lies only a thin film of serous fluid under negative pressure, which lubricates the sliding surfaces and couples each lung to the chest wall. Mucus belongs to the airway lining rather than the pleura, and a normally air-filled cavity would uncouple the lung from the chest wall instead of coupling it.

questions.stem: A stab wound lets air enter the left pleural cavity (pneumothorax). What immediate effect does this have on the left lung?
options: The left lung inflates further, because the extra air increases the pressure gradient into the alveoli.
Nothing changes in the lung, because each side's diaphragm contracts independently of the pleura.
The left lung stiffens and expands, because serous fluid in the cavity is replaced by air.
The trachea seals the left main bronchus, so airflow into the left lung simply stops.
The left lung recoils and collapses, because intrapleural pressure rises toward atmospheric pressure and the coupling between chest wall and lung is lost.
questions.exp: Ventilation depends on the negative pressure of the pleural cavity holding each lung against the chest wall; air entering the cavity abolishes that pressure difference, so the elastic lung recoils and collapses on that side. The further-inflation option mistakes the injury for a stronger ventilatory gradient, and there is no reflex that seals a bronchus.

questions.stem: In human blood, which option gives the approximate shares of carbon dioxide transported as bicarbonate ions, bound to hemoglobin, and dissolved in plasma, respectively?
options: About 23%, about 70%, about 7%.
About 70%, about 23%, about 7%.
About 70%, about 7%, about 23%.
About 97%, about 3%, about 0%.
About 50%, about 43%, about 7%.
questions.exp: Most carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate ions (about 70%), a substantial fraction binds to the globin of hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin (about 23%), and only a small part stays dissolved in plasma (about 7%). The 97 and 3 figures belong to oxygen transport, and swapping the bicarbonate and carbamino shares is the classic slip.
questions.topic: Biology · CO2 transport (share of each form)

questions.stem: Oxygen and carbon dioxide are both carried with the help of hemoglobin. Which statement about their binding sites on hemoglobin is correct?
options: Oxygen binds to the iron of the heme group, while carbon dioxide binds to amino groups of the globin polypeptide chains.
Oxygen binds to the globin chains, while carbon dioxide binds to the iron of the heme group.
Both gases bind to the iron of the heme group and compete for the same site.
Oxygen binds to the heme iron, while carbon dioxide is carried entirely dissolved in plasma with no binding to hemoglobin.
Oxygen binds to the globin chains, while carbon dioxide binds to the cell membrane of the red blood cell.
questions.exp: The heme iron is the site for oxygen, forming oxyhemoglobin, whereas carbon dioxide forms carbaminohemoglobin on amino groups of the globin proteins, so the two gases occupy different parts of the molecule and can be carried at the same time. The shared-site option is the standard error: carbon dioxide does not load onto the heme iron.
questions.topic: Biology · hemoglobin binding sites (heme vs globin)

questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of the oxygen transported in systemic arterial blood is carried bound to hemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin?
questions.exp: Hemoglobin is by far the main oxygen carrier: about 97% of the oxygen in arterial blood rides on hemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin and only about 3% dissolves in the plasma. The 7 and 23 figures belong to the dissolved and carbamino shares of carbon dioxide transport, not to oxygen.

questions.stem: A patient has a severely reduced hemoglobin concentration, yet the partial pressure of oxygen in her arterial blood is normal. Which statement explains why her tissues still receive too little oxygen?
options: Her alveolar walls have become too thick for oxygen to diffuse across at a normal partial pressure.
Dissolved oxygen in plasma normally supplies about 70% of the tissues' demand, so small changes matter greatly.
About 97% of the oxygen in arterial blood is bound to hemoglobin, so with less hemoglobin the total oxygen content of the blood falls even though its partial pressure is normal.
With less hemoglobin, oxygen binds more tightly to the remaining molecules and therefore cannot be released at the tissues.
The dissolved fraction rises until it equals the normal total oxygen content of the blood.
questions.exp: Arterial partial pressure determines how saturated the available hemoglobin becomes, not how much oxygen the blood carries in total; since roughly 97% of oxygen travels on hemoglobin, anemia cuts total delivery while the partial pressure and the small dissolved share stay normal. The tight-binding claim describes a shift of the dissociation curve, not anemia, and normal lung diffusion cannot make up for a lack of carrier.

questions.stem: Emphysema progressively destroys the walls between the pulmonary alveoli. Which direct consequence for gas exchange follows?
options: The total surface area available for gas exchange decreases, so oxygen uptake per breath falls.
The bronchioles constrict by smooth muscle spasm, so air cannot reach the alveoli.
The amount of hemoglobin in the blood falls, so oxygen carriage drops.
The diaphragm can no longer contract, so thoracic volume cannot increase.
The pleural cavity fills with mucus, so the lungs cannot slide along the chest wall.
questions.exp: The alveolar walls are themselves the exchange surface, so merging alveoli into fewer, larger sacs cuts the diffusion area and oxygen uptake falls. Bronchiolar spasm defines asthma, a low hemoglobin count defines anemia, and neither diaphragm function nor pleural fluid is touched by alveolar destruction.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a condition with the structure primarily affected is incorrect?
options: Pleurisy: the pleural membranes.
Myocardial infarction: a coronary artery.
Varicose veins: incompetent valves in the veins of the legs.
Asthma: destruction of the walls between the alveoli.
Chronic bronchitis: the mucus-producing glands of the bronchi.
questions.exp: Asthma is a reversible narrowing of the airways caused by contraction of bronchiolar smooth muscle together with inflammation, not by destruction of alveolar walls, which is the hallmark of emphysema. The other four pairs are correct: pleurisy inflames the pleura, infarction follows a blocked coronary artery, varicose veins involve failing venous valves, and bronchitis involves bronchial mucus glands.

questions.stem: Fatty plaques narrow a patient's coronary arteries. Why is the heart muscle endangered especially during physical exertion?
options: Because the coronary arteries supply the lungs, and exertion raises pulmonary blood flow above what the narrowed vessels can carry.
Because the coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself, and exertion raises the heart's oxygen demand faster than blood flow through the narrowed vessels can increase.
Because exertion diverts all coronary blood flow to the skeletal muscles, leaving the myocardium without perfusion even in healthy people.
Because coronary arteries fill with blood during ventricular systole, and the higher heart rate of exertion shortens systole below what filling needs.
Because the myocardium switches to anaerobic fermentation during exertion, and the narrowed arteries cannot deliver the extra glucose this requires.
questions.exp: The coronary arteries branch from the aorta and feed the heart muscle itself; during exercise the myocardium's oxygen demand climbs steeply, and a stenosed vessel cannot raise its flow enough, so the muscle becomes ischemic. The systole option inverts the timing, since coronary filling occurs mainly during diastole, and the coronary circulation never supplies the lungs.

questions.stem: In the small intestine, the enzyme enterokinase converts pancreatic trypsinogen into active trypsin, and trypsin then activates the other pancreatic proenzymes. A drug that fully inhibits enterokinase is given. Which outcome is expected?
options: All digestion of food in the intestine stops, because every pancreatic enzyme is released as an inactive precursor.
Fat digestion falls to almost zero, because trypsin must first convert prolipase into active lipase.

Protein digestion in the intestine is strongly impaired, because trypsin and the proenzymes it activates stay inactive, while fat and starch digestion continue, since lipase and amylase are secreted already active.
Starch digestion stops, because pancreatic amylase is released as an inactive zymogen that only trypsin can switch on.
Protein digestion ceases entirely, because pepsinogen can no longer be activated without enterokinase.
questions.exp: Only the proteases travel as zymogens; without enterokinase no trypsin forms, so chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidase are never activated either. The prolipase and amylase options fail because lipase and amylase are secreted already active, and pepsinogen is activated by stomach acid, not by enterokinase.

questions.stem: Which statement about bile in human digestion is correct?
options: Bile is produced by the liver and emulsifies fat into fine droplets, enlarging the surface area exposed to lipase, but it hydrolyses no chemical bonds.
Bile is produced by the gallbladder, which synthesises it anew each time a fatty meal reaches the duodenum.
Bile is produced by the liver and digests triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol by means of its own enzymes.
Bile is produced by the pancreas and stored by the liver until a fatty meal arrives.
Bile is produced by the liver and its main digestive role is the breakdown of nucleic acids into nucleotides.
questions.exp: Bile is made by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and released into the duodenum; emulsification is a physical dispersion that enlarges the surface lipase works on, and bile itself contains no digestive enzymes. The option crediting the gallbladder with production names the standard confusion: the gallbladder only stores and concentrates.

questions.stem: A drug almost completely abolishes hydrochloric acid secretion by the stomach. Which outcome follows most directly?
options: The stomach stops secreting pepsinogen altogether, because pepsinogen release is triggered by acid itself.
Gastric protein digestion is unaffected, because pepsinogen activates itself independently of pH once the food is churned.
Gastric fat digestion stops completely, because gastric lipase is active only at pH 2 or below.
Activation of pepsinogen into pepsin is largely prevented, so gastric protein digestion slows, while digestion of protein can still continue in the intestine through pancreatic proteases.
Bile release stops, because the gallbladder contracts only in response to acid produced by the stomach.
questions.exp: Acid both converts pepsinogen to active pepsin and supplies the low pH at which pepsin works, so gastric protein digestion drops. Pepsinogen secretion does not require acid, gastric lipase operates at the moderately acidic pH of the stomach, and gallbladder contraction is driven mainly by cholecystokinin, so the other options overstate or misplace the role of acid.

questions.stem: Rennin (chymosin), secreted by the gastric mucosa of young mammals, turns liquid milk into a solid curd so that it stays longer in the stomach. The substance on which rennin acts is:
options: lactose, the sugar of milk, which is split into glucose and galactose
casein, the main protein of milk, which coagulates in the presence of calcium ions
milk fat, which is dispersed into fine droplets
calcium phosphate dissolved in the milk, which precipitates out
the immunoglobulins of milk, which are degraded so the young can absorb other nutrients
questions.exp: Rennin is a protease: it clots the milk protein casein, with calcium ions stabilising the curd. The lactose option confuses rennin with lactase, and the fat option confuses it with lipase or bile.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about human digestion is false?
options: Pepsin is secreted as the inactive precursor pepsinogen and is activated by the acid environment of the stomach.
Pancreatic juice supplies proteases, amylase, lipase and nucleases, which act in the small intestine.
Bile contains no digestive enzymes, yet efficient fat digestion depends on it.
Salivary amylase starts starch digestion in the mouth, and its action ceases once the food meets the acid stomach.
The gallbladder produces bile in response to the hormone cholecystokinin and releases it into the duodenum.
questions.exp: Cholecystokinin does make the gallbladder contract, but bile is produced by the liver; the gallbladder only stores and concentrates it. The other four statements correctly describe pepsinogen, the contents of pancreatic juice, the enzyme-free role of bile and the fate of salivary amylase.

questions.stem: A treatment destroys most of a patient's thyroid gland, including both the follicular cells and the parafollicular (C) cells, while the four parathyroid glands remain intact. Which outcome is expected?
options: Basal metabolic rate rises, because the thyroid hormones are the hormones that slow metabolism down.
Blood calcium falls to dangerous levels, because calcitonin was the principal hormone that raises blood calcium.
Basal metabolic rate falls, and blood calcium stays close to normal, because parathyroid hormone from the intact parathyroids is the principal regulator of blood calcium.
Basal metabolic rate is unaffected, because the thyroid hormones act only on bone remodelling.
Blood calcium rises uncontrollably, because the loss of calcitonin leaves parathyroid hormone completely unopposed.
questions.exp: The follicular cells secrete T3 and T4, which set the basal metabolic rate, so their loss lowers it. Calcitonin only fine-tunes calcium downward while parathyroid hormone is the dominant regulator, so calcium remains near normal; the option that makes calcitonin the main calcium-raising hormone reverses its action.

questions.stem: Blood tests show that a person's plasma calcium concentration is abnormally high. Which endocrine response is expected?
options: Parathyroid hormone secretion falls and calcitonin secretion rises, favouring the deposition of calcium in bone.
Parathyroid hormone secretion rises, stimulating osteoclasts to release further calcium from bone.
Calcitonin secretion falls, which allows calcium to accumulate still further in the blood.
Both parathyroid hormone and calcitonin secretion fall, because both hormones raise blood calcium.
Insulin secretion falls, because insulin normally removes calcium from the blood along with glucose.
questions.exp: A high calcium level suppresses parathyroid hormone and stimulates calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclasts and favours calcium deposition, restoring the level by negative feedback. The option raising parathyroid hormone describes the response to low calcium, and the claim that both hormones raise calcium is wrong, since parathyroid hormone raises and calcitonin lowers it.

questions.stem: In untreated type 1 diabetes, insulin secretion is nearly absent and blood glucose rises far above the normal renal threshold. Why does glucose appear in the urine?
options: Insulin normally seals the glomerular filter against glucose; without it, glucose filters freely and none of it can be reabsorbed.
High blood glucose triggers the active secretion of glucose from the blood into the distal convoluted tubule.
The sodium-potassium pumps of the proximal tubule fail, so every reabsorptive process in the nephron stops.
The filtered glucose load exceeds the transport capacity of the reabsorption mechanisms in the proximal convoluted tubule, so the surplus escapes reabsorption and is excreted.
The collecting duct destroys glucose molecules, so any glucose reaching it can no longer be recovered.
questions.exp: The proximal convoluted tubule normally reabsorbs essentially all filtered glucose through specific co-transporters, but these have a finite maximum; above the renal threshold the surplus passes on into the urine. Glucose filtration and reabsorption do not depend on insulin, so the option blaming the glomerular filter misstates the mechanism.

questions.stem: During a long fast, glucagon helps to keep the blood glucose level stable. Which statement about this hormone is correct?
options: It triggers glycogen breakdown equally in liver and muscle, so both tissues feed glucose into the blood.
It triggers glycogen breakdown mainly in the liver, while muscle keeps its stores because muscle cells lack glucagon receptors and use their glycogen for their own contraction.
It promotes the uptake of glucose by muscle cells, lowering the blood glucose level during the fast.
It is released by the alpha cells of the pancreas when blood glucose rises after a meal.
It converts muscle glycogen directly into blood glucose before the liver is involved at all.
questions.exp: Glucagon acts chiefly on the liver, driving glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; muscle lacks glucagon receptors, so its glycogen serves local contraction only. The option of equal breakdown in both tissues ignores this receptor distribution, and the claim of release when glucose rises reverses the actual trigger.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the active pumping of sodium ions out of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Which outcome follows?
options: The salt gradient in the medulla weakens, so the collecting duct reabsorbs less water and a large volume of dilute urine is produced, even when ADH is present.
ADH secretion rises and concentrates the urine beyond the normal maximum, fully compensating for the block.
Filtration at the glomerulus stops, because the loop of Henle generates the filtration pressure.
Glucose escapes into the urine, because the loop of Henle is normally where glucose is reabsorbed.
The urine becomes maximally concentrated, because sodium accumulates unchecked in the medulla.
questions.exp: Active sodium transport out of the ascending limb builds the medullary osmotic gradient on which ADH-driven water reabsorption in the collecting duct depends; without it the gradient collapses and dilute urine flows out. No amount of ADH can act on a gradient that no longer exists, and glomerular filtration pressure is independent of the loop.
questions.topic: Biology · nephron (loop of Henle, medullary gradient)

questions.stem: A drug enters the fluid of the kidney tubule by two routes: filtration at the glomerulus, and active transport from the peritubular blood into the tubule. The second route of entry is called:
options: reabsorption
pressure filtration
countercurrent multiplication
dialysis
tubular secretion
questions.exp: Secretion is the active transfer of substances from the peritubular blood into the filtrate, the reverse of reabsorption, which carries substances from the tubule back to the blood. Filtration is the pressure-driven, non-selective process at the glomerulus and cannot describe an active second route.

questions.stem: A healthy person quickly drinks one litre of pure water and plasma osmolarity falls slightly. Which sequence of events follows?
options: ADH release is stimulated, the collecting duct becomes less permeable to water, and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced.
ADH release is suppressed, the collecting duct becomes more permeable to water, and urine output falls.
ADH release is suppressed, the collecting duct becomes less permeable to water, and a large volume of dilute urine is produced.
Aldosterone release stops while ADH stays high, so sodium alone is excreted.
Glomerular filtration ceases until plasma osmolarity returns to normal, so no urine is produced.
questions.exp: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the falling osmolarity and cut ADH release from the posterior pituitary; the collecting duct becomes water-impermeable and the dilute filtrate leaves as copious pale urine. The option that pairs suppression with increased water permeability reverses the effect of ADH, which inserts aquaporins.

questions.stem: Which statement about the cells of bone tissue is correct?
options: Osteoblasts dissolve bone matrix and release calcium, while osteoclasts build new matrix.
Osteoclasts resorb bone matrix, releasing calcium and phosphate into the blood, while osteoblasts deposit new matrix.
Osteocytes are the main cells that form new bone matrix during growth.
Chondrocytes resorb calcified matrix in order to release stored calcium.
Osteoclasts end up trapped in lacunae as mature cells that maintain the matrix.
questions.exp: Osteoclasts resorb bone and osteoblasts deposit osteoid, and the balance between them, steered by parathyroid hormone and calcitonin, sets blood calcium. The first option swaps the two roles, the usual confusion, while the trapped-in-lacunae description belongs to osteocytes.

questions.stem: A toxin blocks the voltage-gated potassium channels of a neuron but leaves all other channels and the sodium-potassium pump intact. Which outcome follows when the axon is stimulated above threshold?
options: Depolarisation still occurs, but repolarisation is delayed because K⁺ efflux is blocked, so the membrane stays depolarised far longer and cannot carry rapid repeated impulses.
No depolarisation occurs, because the rising phase of the action potential is driven by potassium leaving the cell.
The action potential runs normally, because the rising phase depends on chloride and the falling phase on sodium.
The membrane repolarises faster than normal, because the sodium channels stay open for longer.
The resting potential is lost at once, because the resting membrane potential is maintained by voltage-gated potassium channels.
questions.exp: The upstroke of the action potential uses voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and the falling phase uses voltage-gated K⁺ channels; blocking the latter leaves the membrane depolarised and prolongs the refractory period. The last option fails because the resting potential is set by potassium leak through non-gated channels together with the pump, not by gated channels.

questions.stem: A poison blocks the voltage-gated calcium channels in the presynaptic terminal of a chemical synapse, while impulse conduction along the axon itself is normal. Which outcome follows?
options: The action potential fails to travel along the presynaptic axon, because calcium carries the impulse current there.
Neurotransmitter is released continuously, even without impulses, and permanently stimulates the postsynaptic cell.
The postsynaptic cell depolarises normally, because transmission at chemical synapses is electrical rather than chemical.
The impulse still arrives at the terminal, but vesicle fusion with the membrane is not triggered, so the postsynaptic cell receives no chemical signal.
Reuptake of neurotransmitter stops, so the synapse becomes overstimulated by transmitter left in the cleft.
questions.exp: Ca²⁺ entry is the coupling step between the arriving action potential and the fusion of transmitter vesicles; blocking it silences transmission while conduction remains intact. The overstimulation option describes blocked reuptake or breakdown, a different lesion, and chemical synapses are not electrical.

questions.stem: A disease progressively destroys the myelin sheath of peripheral motor axons. Which chain of consequences follows for a signal travelling toward the muscle?
options: The impulse travels faster, because bare membrane conducts electrical current more readily than insulated membrane.
The impulse continues normally, because saltatory conduction is an optional shortcut rather than a necessity.

The impulse slows and then fails to reach the terminal, because the demyelinated stretches of membrane lack the dense voltage-gated sodium channels needed to regenerate the signal, so muscle activation weakens.
The resting potential reverses along the whole axon at once, producing continuous contraction.
Neurotransmitter release increases automatically to compensate, keeping muscle activation normal.
questions.exp: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels sit at the nodes of Ranvier, so only there can the signal regenerate itself; across a demyelinated stretch the local current decays below threshold and conduction fails. The faster-conduction option inverts the role of insulation, which forces the impulse to jump node to node at high speed.

questions.stem: A patient is given a drug that mimics acetylcholine at the receptors of the parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system. Which set of effects is expected?
options: Heart rate rises, pupils dilate, airways widen and digestive activity is inhibited.
Heart rate falls, pupils constrict, airways narrow and digestive activity is stimulated.
Heart rate falls, pupils dilate, airways widen and digestive activity is stimulated.
Heart rate rises, pupils constrict, airways narrow and digestive activity is inhibited.
Heart rate falls, pupils constrict, airways widen and digestive activity is inhibited.
questions.exp: The parasympathetic division is the rest-and-digest state: it slows the heart, constricts the pupils, narrows the airways and promotes gut motility and secretion. The option with raised heart rate and dilated pupils lists sympathetic effects, and each remaining option mixes one effect of one division with the effects of the other.

questions.stem: A person walks from bright sunshine into a dim cinema, sees almost nothing at first and regains useful vision over several minutes. Which explanation is correct?
options: Bright light destroyed the cones, and new ones must be produced by cell division before vision returns.
In dim light the lens changes shape so that more light is admitted directly into the eye.
The pupil reaches its maximum diameter at once, so vision should be sharp immediately.
Bright light bleached the pigment of the photoreceptors packed in the fovea, where dim vision is normally sharpest.
In bright light the rod pigment rhodopsin was largely bleached and the cones did most of the work; in darkness rhodopsin is resynthesised over minutes and the rods gradually take over.
questions.exp: Rhodopsin in the rods is bleached by bright light and takes minutes to regenerate, matching the timescale of dark adaptation, while the cones serve bright-light vision. The fovea option fails because the fovea contains only cones, and the lens focuses light rather than controlling how much of it enters.

questions.stem: Which statement about the organisation of the human nervous system is correct?
options: The central nervous system consists of brain and spinal cord, while the peripheral nervous system divides into the somatic and autonomic systems, the latter carrying sympathetic and parasympathetic branches.
The sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions are subdivisions of the somatic nervous system.
The autonomic nervous system lies entirely within the brain and spinal cord.
The spinal cord belongs to the peripheral nervous system, because peripheral nerves run through it.
The autonomic nervous system controls the contraction of skeletal muscles during voluntary movements.
questions.exp: The CNS is brain plus spinal cord; the PNS splits into the somatic system (voluntary, skeletal muscle) and the autonomic system (involuntary control of smooth and cardiac muscle and glands), which carries the two named branches. Placing the autonomic branches under the somatic system, or crediting the autonomic system with voluntary skeletal muscle control, mixes the divisions up.
questions.topic: Biology · nervous system divisions (CNS and PNS)

questions.stem: A lumbar puncture is performed to sample the fluid that cushions the brain and spinal cord. The needle passes through the dura mater and then through one further meningeal layer before reaching the fluid. Which layer is pierced last, and which fluid is sampled?
options: the pia mater, and the sample is tissue fluid from the subdural space
the dura mater, and the sample is lymph from the epidural space
the arachnoid mater, and the sample is blood from the subdural space
the arachnoid mater, and the sample is cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space
the pia mater, and the sample is cerebrospinal fluid from the subdural space
questions.exp: From outside inwards the meninges run dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater, and cerebrospinal fluid fills the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia, so the arachnoid is the last layer crossed. The subdural options place the fluid in a space that normally contains essentially none.

questions.stem: In an animal experiment both vagus nerves are cut, and the animal is observed after recovery from the surgery. Which set of consequences is expected?
options: Heart rate falls, because the vagus carries the main sympathetic acceleration of the heart.
Heart rate is unchanged, because the heartbeat is driven entirely by the sinoatrial node itself.
Heart rate rises above normal, because the tonic parasympathetic slowing exerted by the vagus is lost, while digestive motility and secretion decrease.
Digestive activity accelerates, because the vagus normally inhibits the gut.
The pupils dilate permanently, because the vagus supplies the muscles of the iris.
questions.exp: The vagus carries parasympathetic fibres that keep a constant brake on the heart and stimulate digestive activity; cutting it releases the brake and withdraws the stimulus, so the heart speeds up and the gut slows. The unchanged-heart option ignores this resting parasympathetic tone, and the iris is not supplied by the vagus.
questions.topic: Biology · vagus nerve and autonomic control

questions.stem: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) catalyses the committed step of glycolysis. Which of the following statements about its control is false?
options: ATP binds to an allosteric regulatory site on PFK-1 and lowers the enzyme's activity.
AMP binds to PFK-1 and relieves the inhibition caused by high ATP.
Citrate, an intermediate of the citric acid cycle, allosterically inhibits PFK-1.
ATP acts only as an inhibitor of PFK-1 and plays no role whatsoever as its substrate.
A high AMP:ATP ratio in the cytosol favours flux through the PFK-1 step.
questions.exp: PFK-1 uses ATP to phosphorylate fructose-6-phosphate, so ATP is a substrate at the active site as well as an allosteric inhibitor at a separate regulatory site. AMP and citrate act exactly as the other statements describe, so the claim denying ATP any substrate role is the false one.

questions.stem: During a sprint, the ATP concentration inside a fast muscle fibre falls and its AMP concentration rises. What is the most likely immediate effect on glycolysis in that fibre?
options: Glycolysis accelerates, because AMP allosterically activates PFK-1, the enzyme catalysing the committed step.
Glycolysis stops, because PFK-1 requires ATP as an allosteric activator.
Glycolysis continues at the same rate, because AMP has no effect on glycolytic enzymes.
Glycolysis slows, because AMP competes with glucose for hexokinase at the entry to the pathway.
Glycolysis accelerates, because AMP directly phosphorylates ADP to make extra ATP inside the enzyme.
questions.exp: AMP signals a low energy charge and allosterically activates PFK-1, so the committed step speeds up even though cellular ATP has fallen. The claim that PFK-1 needs ATP as an activator inverts the real control: ATP at high concentration inhibits, while a small amount serves only as substrate.
questions.topic: Biology · PFK-1 and the AMP:ATP ratio

questions.stem: In the aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule, what do the two link reactions (oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate) together yield, and where do they occur?
options: 2 acetyl-CoA, 4 CO₂ and 2 NADH, inside the mitochondrial matrix
2 acetyl-CoA, 2 CO₂ and 2 NADH, inside the mitochondrial matrix
2 acetyl-CoA, 2 CO₂ and 2 FADH₂, on the inner mitochondrial membrane
1 acetyl-CoA, 1 CO₂ and 1 NADH, inside the mitochondrial matrix
2 acetyl-CoA, 2 CO₂ and 2 NADH, in the cytosol
questions.exp: Each of the two pyruvates from one glucose loses one carbon as CO₂ and reduces one NAD⁺ to NADH while being joined to coenzyme A, so together the link reactions give 2 acetyl-CoA, 2 CO₂ and 2 NADH. The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex sits in the mitochondrial matrix, so the cytosol option confuses this step with glycolysis.

questions.stem: A toxin irreversibly inhibits the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex in cells that are supplied only with glucose. Which outcome follows?
options: Pyruvate accumulates, acetyl-CoA production falls and the ATP yield from glucose oxidation drops sharply.
Pyruvate accumulates but the citric acid cycle speeds up to compensate, keeping ATP output normal.
Acetyl-CoA accumulates and activates the citric acid cycle, raising ATP output.
Glycolysis stops, because pyruvate dehydrogenase catalyses an essential step of glycolysis itself.
The electron transport chain accelerates, because NADH from glycolysis alone floods into the mitochondria.
questions.exp: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is the gateway between cytosolic glycolysis and the mitochondrial citric acid cycle, so blocking it starves the cycle of acetyl-CoA, cutting NADH and FADH₂ generation and with them the ATP yield. Glycolysis itself is unaffected, which is why pyruvate piles up, and the respiratory chain slows rather than accelerates because it runs short of electron supply.

questions.stem: What are the products of one complete turn of the citric acid cycle?
options: 2 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂
4 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 1 CO₂
3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 2 CO₂
3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP by oxidative phosphorylation and 2 CO₂
3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP and 1 CO₂
questions.exp: One turn reduces three NAD⁺ to NADH and one FAD to FADH₂, generates one GTP by substrate-level phosphorylation and releases two CO₂. Counting two FADH₂ overstates the single FAD-dependent step, and the GTP is not a product of oxidative phosphorylation.

questions.stem: Acetyl-CoA labelled with ¹⁴C on its methyl (CH₃) carbon enters the citric acid cycle. When is the label first released as ¹⁴CO₂?
options: During the first turn of the cycle, as one of the two CO₂ molecules released
During the second turn, after the label has passed into oxaloacetate
Immediately on entry, because citrate synthase decarboxylates acetyl-CoA as it condenses
From the third turn onwards: neither carbon of the entering acetyl group is released during the first turn, and the methyl carbon survives even longer than the carbonyl carbon
Never, because the methyl carbon is fully conserved for as long as the cycle runs
questions.exp: The two CO₂ released in any turn come from carbons that were part of oxaloacetate, so an incoming acetyl group survives its first complete passage intact; with a ¹⁴C label the carbonyl carbon appears in CO₂ mainly in the second turn and the methyl carbon mainly from the third turn onwards. Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate without any decarboxylation, so the immediate-release option misunderstands that step.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the citric acid cycle is false?
options: The cycle runs mainly in the mitochondrial matrix, with succinate dehydrogenase embedded in the inner membrane.
Succinate dehydrogenase transfers electrons from succinate to FAD, and the resulting FADH₂ passes them on directly within the respiratory chain.
The GTP formed in the cycle is produced by substrate-level phosphorylation.
Acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate, which is regenerated at the end of every turn.
Each turn of the cycle consumes two molecules of acetyl-CoA and regenerates one molecule of oxaloacetate.
questions.exp: A single turn oxidises one acetyl group and regenerates the oxaloacetate carrier, so the two-acetyl-CoA claim confuses per-turn and per-glucose accounting. The other claims hold: succinate dehydrogenase is the cycle's membrane-bound enzyme and hands its FADH₂ electrons straight to ubiquinone, and the GTP arises by substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the mitochondrial electron transport chain is false?
options: Complex I transfers electrons from NADH to ubiquinone and pumps protons to the intermembrane space.
The final electron acceptor for the electrons carried by NADH is cytochrome c of complex III.
Complex II transfers electrons from succinate, via FADH₂, to ubiquinone without pumping protons.
Complex III passes electrons from ubiquinol to cytochrome c and pumps protons.
Complex IV transfers electrons to O₂, reducing it to water, and pumps protons.
questions.exp: Cytochrome c is only an intermediate shuttle between complexes III and IV, so the electrons carried by NADH end on O₂ at complex IV, not on cytochrome c. The remaining statements match the standard division of labour, including complex II feeding ubiquinone without pumping protons, the very reason FADH₂ electrons bypass complex I.

questions.stem: Rotenone specifically blocks electron transfer at complex I of the respiratory chain. A respiring cell is then supplied with succinate as its main oxidisable substrate. Which outcome is expected?
options: ATP synthesis continues at a reduced rate, because electrons from succinate FADH₂ enter the chain at complex II and drive pumping at complexes III and IV.
ATP synthesis stops completely, because every electron entering the chain must first pass through complex I.
ATP synthesis continues at the normal rate, because complex II pumps protons and takes over the work of complex I.
The proton gradient rises above its normal value, because succinate oxidation pumps more protons than NADH oxidation.
Oxygen consumption stops completely, even though the proton gradient persists.
questions.exp: Succinate oxidation passes electrons to ubiquinone through complex II, leaving the blocked complex I out of the circuit, so complexes III and IV still pump protons and ATP synthesis continues, though at a lower rate because complex I's contribution is lost. Complex II pumps no protons, so the gradient cannot rise above normal, and with succinate feeding the chain oxygen consumption continues rather than stopping.

questions.stem: Cyanide binds the Fe³⁺ of cytochrome a₃ in complex IV and halts electron transfer to oxygen. In a mitochondrion poisoned in this way, what happens?
options: Complexes I, II and III become fully oxidised while NADH accumulates in the matrix.
Proton pumping continues at complexes I and III even though complex IV is blocked.
Complexes I, II and III become fully reduced, proton pumping stops and ATP synthesis falls to zero.
The proton gradient is unaffected, because ATP synthase can still run in reverse.
Oxygen consumption continues at a lower rate while NAD⁺ is steadily regenerated.
questions.exp: With the final acceptor blocked, electrons pile up behind complex IV, trapping complexes I, II and III in their reduced states, stopping all proton pumping and letting the gradient drain until ATP synthase has nothing left to exploit. The mirror-image option, fully oxidised upstream carriers with accumulating NADH, describes exactly what cannot happen, since oxidising NADH is what stops.

questions.stem: A molecule that makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons is added to actively respiring mitochondria. Which outcome is expected?
options: Electron transport stops, because the proton gradient is the driving force for electron flow.
ATP synthesis continues at its normal rate, because ATP synthase is not part of the electron transport chain.
ATP synthesis increases, because protons now return to the matrix faster.
Electron transport slows down, while ATP synthesis is unaffected.
Electron transport and oxygen consumption speed up, most of the released energy appears as heat, and ATP synthesis falls.
questions.exp: The leak dissipates the proton gradient that limits electron flow, so the chain and oxygen consumption speed up, but the energy escapes as heat instead of turning ATP synthase, which is exactly how brown fat thermogenesis works. Faster proton return cannot raise ATP output, because the stored energy is dissipated rather than harnessed.

questions.stem: Per molecule delivered to the respiratory chain, FADH₂ yields roughly two ATP, whereas NADH yields roughly two to three times as many. What is the main reason for the difference?
options: FADH₂ enters the chain at complex II, so its electrons bypass complex I and its oxidation pumps fewer protons.
FADH₂ carries only one electron, whereas NADH carries two.
FADH₂ cannot be reoxidised inside the mitochondrion and is excreted from the cell.
FADH₂ donates its electrons directly to oxygen at complex IV.
FADH₂ releases its electrons into the intermembrane space, where they cannot reach the chain.
questions.exp: FADH₂ delivers its electrons to ubiquinone at complex II, which pumps no protons, so those electrons skip the proton-pumping step of complex I and store less energy in the gradient. Both carriers carry two electrons, so a difference in electron count cannot explain the lower yield.
questions.topic: Biology · NADH and FADH₂ entry points

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the roles of NAD⁺, FAD and ATP in metabolism is correct?
options: ATP accepts electrons from oxidised substrates and passes them on to the electron transport chain.
NAD⁺ and FAD store the energy they harvest as a proton gradient inside their own rings.
FAD accepts two electrons and two protons during glycolysis, while NAD⁺ accepts single electrons only.
NAD⁺ and FAD accept electrons, together with protons, from oxidised substrates, while ATP transfers usable energy mainly through its terminal phosphate bond.
ATP is reduced to ADP when it transfers its terminal phosphate group to a substrate.
questions.exp: NAD⁺ and FAD are the electron and hydrogen acceptors of dehydrogenase reactions, while ATP is the currency that moves energy through its terminal phosphate, two distinct roles. Phosphate transfer is not a redox event, so describing ATP as reduced to ADP misapplies the term.
questions.topic: Biology · NAD⁺, FAD and ATP as carriers

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about alcoholic fermentation in yeast is correct?
options: Pyruvate is reduced directly to ethanol, so no CO₂ is produced.
Alcoholic fermentation generates extra ATP beyond glycolysis by substrate-level phosphorylation.
Pyruvate is first decarboxylated to acetaldehyde with release of CO₂, then reduced to ethanol by NADH, regenerating NAD⁺ with no further ATP synthesis.
Yeast regenerates NAD⁺ during fermentation using lactate dehydrogenase.
The NADH that reduces acetaldehyde is supplied by the electron transport chain running in reverse.
questions.exp: Yeast first decarboxylates pyruvate to acetaldehyde, releasing the CO₂ of fermentation, and alcohol dehydrogenase then spends glycolytic NADH reducing acetaldehyde to ethanol, which is precisely how NAD⁺ is regenerated for further glycolysis; neither fermentation step makes ATP. Lactate dehydrogenase is the muscle route, and the NADH used comes from glycolysis in the cytosol, not from a reversed respiratory chain.

questions.stem: A muscle fibre metabolises glucose entirely by glycolysis followed by lactic acid fermentation. What is the net ATP yield per glucose, and why does fermentation remain indispensable?
options: 2 ATP: fermentation regenerates the NAD⁺ that glycolysis needs at the step oxidising glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate.
4 ATP: the fermentation steps themselves produce two extra ATP per pyruvate.
8 ATP: the conversion of pyruvate to lactate feeds electrons into the electron transport chain.
0 ATP: glycolysis cannot even start without oxygen.
6 ATP: fermentation converts the NADH of glycolysis into ATP inside the mitochondria.
questions.exp: Glycolysis spends 2 ATP and recovers 4, and converting pyruvate to lactate reoxidises that NADH back to NAD⁺, so the pathway can keep running without oxygen for a net of 2 ATP per glucose. The extra-ATP option is the classic error: the fermentation steps themselves produce no ATP at all.

questions.stem: During skeletal muscle contraction, what is the role of ATP at the moment a myosin head detaches from actin?
options: ATP phosphorylates actin so that myosin can bind it again at a fresh site.
ATP binding to the myosin head weakens its grip on actin and causes detachment; hydrolysis of that ATP then re-cocks the head for the next stroke.
Calcium released by ATP detaches myosin from actin.
ATP is consumed only at the end of the power stroke, to pull the filaments past each other.
Detachment requires no ATP, because the release of ADP alone breaks the cross-bridge.
questions.exp: ATP binding to the myosin head weakens its attachment to actin and detaches the cross-bridge, and the energy of the following hydrolysis re-cocks the head into its high-energy position; without ATP the bridges stay locked, as in rigor mortis. Calcium's role is regulatory, exposing myosin-binding sites through troponin and tropomyosin, not releasing heads.

questions.stem: Dystrophin is absent or non-functional in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. What is its normal role in a skeletal muscle fibre?
options: It binds calcium to troponin, exposing the myosin-binding sites on actin.
It hydrolyses ATP to supply the power stroke of myosin.
It forms the thick filaments of the sarcomere together with myosin.
It stores oxygen inside the fibre, as myoglobin does.
It anchors the actin cytoskeleton to membrane glycoproteins, stabilising the sarcolemma during contraction.
questions.exp: Dystrophin links the sub-sarcolemmal actin network to the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex of the membrane, so losing it lets the sarcolemma tear under the mechanical stress of repeated contraction, which underlies Duchenne muscular dystrophy. ATP hydrolysis belongs to myosin and oxygen storage to myoglobin, so those options assign other proteins' jobs to a structural linker.

questions.stem: A muscle biopsy from an athlete shows fibres rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, with few glycogen granules and strong resistance to fatigue. Which fibre type is this, and in which sport would such fibres predominate?
options: Type II fast glycolytic fibres, as in a sprinter
Type II fast glycolytic fibres, as in a marathon runner
Type I slow oxidative fibres, as in a sprinter
Type I slow oxidative fibres, as in a marathon runner
Cardiac muscle fibres, as in a long-distance swimmer
questions.exp: Dense mitochondria and abundant myoglobin with little stored glycogen are the signature of type I slow oxidative fibres, built for continuous aerobic work and therefore predominant in endurance athletes such as marathon runners. The sprinter pairing is the trap: fast glycolytic fibres depend on glycolysis, are relatively pale and fatigue rapidly.
questions.topic: Biology · fibre type I versus type II
